VAULT-141: One of ten paintings, each over three metres tall, that af Klint made in 1907 to trace a human life from childhood to old age. She said spirits guided her hand. She asked that her abstract work stay hidden for twenty years after her death, and it mostly did. She died in 1944.
VAULT-124: A scene from an album of thirty paintings of city life and secret romance, now a national treasure kept at the Kansong Art Museum in Seoul. Almost nothing certain is known about Sin Yun-bok's life. The poem on the wall says, roughly, that only the two of them know what is in their hearts.
VAULT-151: Atkins laid seaweed straight onto light-sensitive paper and left it in the sun, with no camera involved. Her Photographs of British Algae, begun in 1843, is generally counted as the first book illustrated with photographs. She learned the cyanotype process from its inventor, John Herschel, a family friend.
VAULT-158: Hildegard was an abbess, composer and visionary on the Rhine. Scivias, meaning 'Know the Ways', records twenty-six of her visions, and this opening picture shows her receiving one as flames on her head while a monk takes notes. The original manuscript vanished in 1945. The image survives because nuns at her abbey had painted an exact copy by hand in the years before.
VAULT-132: A nkisi nkondi was made to be used. Among the Kongo peoples, each nail or blade driven into the figure marks an oath sworn, a dispute settled or a plea for help. A ritual specialist, the nganga, activated it with medicines packed into a cavity in the body.
VAULT-135: Kuindzhi showed this painting by itself in a darkened room in St Petersburg in 1880, lit by a lamp. People queued in the street to get in, and some reportedly checked behind the canvas for a hidden light. A grand duke bought it and took it with him on a sea voyage, and the sea air damaged the paint.
VAULT-138: Coatlicue is the Aztec earth goddess, mother of the war god Huitzilopochtli. Her skirt is woven snakes and her necklace is hands and hearts. The statue stands over two and a half metres tall. It was dug up in Mexico City's main square in 1790, and colonial authorities found it alarming enough to bury it again.
VAULT-145: A scene from the Kalevala, Finland's national epic. The old hero Väinämöinen has stolen the Sampo, a magical object that brings wealth to whoever holds it, and the witch Louhi comes after his boat in the form of a giant bird. Gallen-Kallela painted it while Finland was still under Russian rule and looking hard for its own stories.
VAULT-142: From a series of swan paintings af Klint made in 1914 and 1915. It begins with a black swan and a white one meeting beak to beak, and over twenty-four canvases the birds break down into pure geometry. This is one of the later ones.
VAULT-127: Korean folk paintings like this were made by anonymous artists and hung at New Year to keep bad luck out and bring good news in. The magpie is the messenger. The tiger is usually drawn as comical, not fearsome, and the pair is often read as commoners mocking the powerful.
VAULT-136: Inspired by Lermontov's long poem The Demon, about a fallen angel who is more lonely than evil. Vrubel laid the paint on in flat, broken strokes with a palette knife, so the surface looks like mosaic or cut stone. He returned to the Demon again and again for the rest of his working life.
VAULT-139: Angels dressed as Spanish gentlemen and armed with a matchlock gun are a type of painting found only in the colonial Andes. The best-known set hangs in the church at Calamarca in Bolivia, by a painter whose name is lost. This one comes from his circle. The Latin title means, roughly, 'Fear of God'.
VAULT-137: By the traditional account, Ivan the Terrible struck his son and heir with his staff in a fit of rage in 1581 and killed him. Repin paints the second after. Tsar Alexander III had the picture taken off public view for a few months in 1885. It has been attacked by visitors twice, with a knife in 1913 and a metal pole in 2018.
VAULT-125: From the same album as Lovers Under the Moon. Sin Yun-bok painted the night life of the Korean capital, the young gentlemen and the professional entertainers called gisaeng, which earlier court painters had mostly left alone.
VAULT-140: Velasco is Mexico's great landscape painter, best known for his enormous views across the Valley of Mexico. He was also a serious naturalist who drew plants and animals for scientific journals and published a study of the axolotl.
VAULT-152: Haeckel was a German biologist and Darwin's loudest champion in Europe. His Art Forms in Nature, a hundred plates published between 1899 and 1904, fed straight into Art Nouveau design. One of the jellyfish on this plate he named after his first wife, Anna Sethe, who had died young.
VAULT-154: From the Harmonia Macrocosmica, a star atlas published in Amsterdam in 1660 and often called the most beautiful ever made. It lays out the competing models of the universe side by side. This plate shows the one that turned out to be right, with the sun in the middle.
VAULT-155: Piranesi trained as an architect and built almost nothing. He made his name with etchings of Rome instead. The Imaginary Prisons, sixteen plates of staircases and machinery that lead nowhere, first appeared around 1750. About ten years later he reworked every plate to make it darker and more crowded, and that is the version shown here.
VAULT-157: The ceiling of a hall in the Alhambra, the palace of the last Muslim rulers of Spain, in Granada. The honeycomb effect is called muqarnas. It is built from thousands of small plaster cells, each one carved and fitted by hand, so that a solid dome seems to dissolve into light.
VAULT-159: From the Splendor Solis, 'Splendour of the Sun', the most lavish alchemy manuscript to survive. This copy was made in Germany in 1582 and is now in the British Library. The peacock in the flask stands for a stage in the alchemist's work when the mixture was said to flash with every colour.
VAULT-162: On the desert coast of southern Peru, the Paracas people buried their dead wrapped in layer on layer of embroidered cloth. Hundreds of these bundles were excavated in the 1920s. The air there is so dry that the colours have lasted more than two thousand years.
VAULT-163: Morris got the idea from the thrushes that kept stealing strawberries from his kitchen garden. The pattern is printed by a slow, difficult method using indigo that took him years to get right, which made it one of his most expensive cottons. It has been in production more or less ever since.
VAULT-164: The dolphin and anchor was the trademark of Aldus Manutius, the great printer of Renaissance Venice. He took it from an ancient Roman coin. The motto that went with it means 'make haste slowly'. Publishers have been borrowing the mark ever since.
VAULT-165: In 1501 Aldus Manutius printed a Virgil small enough to carry in a pocket, in a slanted new typeface cut for him by Francesco Griffo. That type is the first italic. The small format caught on fast, and it is the ancestor of the paperback.
VAULT-166: The Mainz Psalter of 1457 is the first printed book to say who printed it and when, and the first with initials printed in colour. Johann Fust had been Gutenberg's financial backer. He sued him, took over the equipment, and went into business with Gutenberg's foreman, Peter Schöffer.
VAULT-169: A love song written out in the shape of a heart. It comes from a manuscript of around 1400 full of fiendishly difficult music. The composer's name was Cordier, and 'cor' is Latin for heart. The notes in red tell the singer the rhythm is about to shift.
VAULT-170: Posada made this around 1910 for a cheap printed broadside. She began as a joke about Mexicans who put on European airs: a skeleton in a fancy French hat. Diego Rivera gave her a full body and the name Catrina in a mural in 1947. She is now the face of the Day of the Dead.
VAULT-171: Senjafuda means 'thousand-shrine tags'. Pilgrims in Japan pasted slips printed with their names onto the gates and ceilings of temples and shrines they visited. In Edo the slips turned into a collecting craze, with clubs that met to trade ever fancier designs.
VAULT-172: Richard Pynson came from Normandy and became one of the first printers in London, and then printer to King Henry VIII. In 1509 he was the first in England to use roman type, the upright letterforms that are still standard.
VAULT-173: Korean potters of the Goryeo period made celadon that even Chinese visitors admitted was among the best in the world. This incense burner is a national treasure of Korea. The base rests on the backs of three tiny rabbits.
VAULT-175: Wang Ximeng painted this scroll, nearly twelve metres long, when he was eighteen. He had been taught by the emperor Huizong himself. It is the only work of his that survives, and he is thought to have died within a few years of finishing it. The blues and greens are ground azurite and malachite.
VAULT-176: Pakal came to the throne of the Maya city of Palenque at twelve and ruled for sixty-eight years. His tomb was found in 1952, deep inside a pyramid, at the bottom of a hidden staircase. The mask, made of more than three hundred pieces of jade, was stolen from a Mexico City museum in 1985 and recovered four years later.
VAULT-177: A group of brass and copper heads was dug up at Ife, in what is now Nigeria, in 1938. They were so naturalistic and so well cast that some Europeans at the time refused to believe Africans had made them. They had been made there, by Yoruba artists, around six hundred years earlier.
VAULT-178: In 1986 workers digging clay near Sanxingdui in Sichuan hit two pits packed with bronzes, jades and elephant tusks, most of them deliberately broken and burned. Among them were bronze heads, some with a mask of gold foil over the face. The people who made them left no writing.
VAULT-179: Half of a pair of folding screens in the Nezu Museum in Tokyo, a national treasure of Japan. Kōrin used two colours on a field of gold leaf and nothing else. Educated viewers would have caught the reference to a famous episode in the Tales of Ise, where a traveller stops by a marsh of irises and thinks of home.
VAULT-180: Berthe Hoola van Nooten was a Dutch woman left widowed and short of money in Java. She drew the island's fruits and flowers and had them published in Brussels in the 1860s as large colour prints, in a book she hoped would support her family.
VAULT-181: Nainsukh, whose name means 'delight of the eyes', came from a family of painters in the hill town of Guler and is widely considered the finest of the Pahari painters. This small painting is generally identified as a self-portrait from early in his career. He went on to spend about twenty years working for a single patron, a minor prince named Balwant Singh.
VAULT-182: Marianne North was a Victorian traveller with no formal training who went round the world painting plants in oils, on the spot. Her gallery at Kew Gardens, which she paid for herself, holds more than eight hundred of her pictures. This pitcher plant from Borneo was unknown to science until she painted it, and it was named after her.
VAULT-183: From later editions of Merian's great book on the insects of Suriname, first published in 1705. She had spent two years in the rainforest there with her younger daughter, paying her own way, until illness forced her home. Plates of reptiles like this one were added to the book after her death.
VAULT-184: Rousseau's last painting, finished in 1910, a few months before he died. He explained that the woman on the sofa is asleep in Paris and dreaming she has been carried off to the jungle. It hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
VAULT-185: The figure is Urizen, a character from Blake's private mythology who measures and limits the world. Blake printed the image as the opening page of one of his books and coloured each copy by hand. He is said to have been colouring one more a few days before he died.
VAULT-190: Dürer never saw a rhinoceros. One had arrived in Lisbon in 1515, the first in Europe since Roman times, and he worked from a written description and a sketch sent to Germany. The animal drowned in a shipwreck on its way to the Pope. Dürer's armour-plated version stayed in textbooks for well over two hundred years.
VAULT-194: Rembrandt scratched this straight into the copper with a needle, a technique that gives rich, velvety lines and wears out after a few dozen prints. When the plate wore down he did not retire it. He reworked the whole image, burying most of the crowd in darkness, so early and late impressions look like two different works.
VAULT-195: Hercules Seghers treated printmaking as an experiment. He printed in coloured inks on tinted paper and sometimes on cloth, then painted over the results, so almost no two impressions are alike. He died poor. Rembrandt admired him and owned eight of his paintings.
VAULT-186: In the Book of Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is punished for his pride by losing his mind and living like an animal, eating grass. Blake shows him on all fours. It is one of a group of twelve large colour prints Blake began in 1795.
VAULT-191: Painted in watercolour in 1502, and still one of the most closely observed animals in art. There is a window reflected in the hare's eye. It belongs to the Albertina in Vienna, which rarely puts the original on show because the colours are so sensitive to light.
VAULT-196: Hogarth published these two as a pair in 1751, priced low so that ordinary people could afford them, in support of a law to restrict the sale of cheap gin. On Beer Street everyone is fat, busy and cheerful. On Gin Lane the only business doing well is the pawnbroker.
VAULT-197: From the Disparates, or Follies, the last and strangest of Goya's print series. He made them privately and never published them. The plates sat in storage and were first printed in 1864, thirty-six years after he died. Nobody knows what order he meant them in or exactly what they mean.
VAULT-201: A scene from a popular story about Princess Takiyasha, daughter of a defeated rebel lord, who calls up a giant skeleton to frighten off an official of the emperor. The print is three sheets wide. The skeleton is anatomically correct, which suggests Kuniyoshi had got hold of a European medical book.
VAULT-187: Blake was no admirer of Isaac Newton. He shows him naked on the seabed, bent over a diagram with his compasses, so absorbed in measuring that he does not notice the rock behind him is alive with colour. A huge bronze based on this figure now sits outside the British Library.
VAULT-192: A study for the hands of an apostle in an altarpiece Dürer painted for a Frankfurt merchant. The altarpiece was destroyed in a fire in 1729, and the drawing is what remains. The popular story that these are the hands of a brother who worked in the mines to pay for Dürer's training has no basis.
VAULT-202: Yoshitoshi is usually called the last great master of the Japanese woodblock print. He worked while photography and Western printing were taking over. One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, published between 1885 and 1892, was his final major series.
VAULT-198: Goya lived through Napoleon's occupation of Spain and recorded it in eighty-odd prints that were too dangerous to publish. They came out in 1863, thirty-five years after his death. The man here has been garrotted. The knife hung round his neck was his crime. Just owning one was enough.
VAULT-203: The third of the three famous prints from Hokusai's Fuji series, with the Great Wave and Red Fuji. The summit sits in clear sky while lightning breaks over the slopes far below. The series was advertised as thirty-six views and sold so well that the publisher added ten more.
VAULT-188: Blake said he saw visions all his life. Around 1819 his friend John Varley, a painter and astrologer, sat up with him at night and asked him to draw what appeared. One of the visitors was the ghost of a flea. The painting is tiny, smaller than a sheet of writing paper, on a wooden panel.
VAULT-205: The tree was a real one, a famous old plum in a garden in Edo whose branches ran along the ground and earned it the name Sleeping Dragon. Hiroshige pushes it right up against the picture so it cuts across everything else. Van Gogh copied this print in oils in 1887.
VAULT-206: Three real celebrities of Edo in the early 1790s: two teahouse waitresses, Okita and Ohisa, and a geisha, Toyohina. Utamaro tells them apart by the family crests on their clothes, and, if you look closely, by small differences in their faces.
VAULT-199: Around 1820 Goya, deaf and in his seventies, covered the walls of his house outside Madrid with fourteen dark paintings. He gave them no titles and, as far as anyone knows, never intended them to be seen. They were cut out of the plaster and moved to canvas fifty years later, and now hang in the Prado.
VAULT-204: After the colour prints, Hokusai made three small books of a hundred more views of Fuji, printed only in black and grey. Many people think they are his best work. At the back he added a short note saying that nothing he drew before seventy was much good and that he expected to improve.
VAULT-189: One of four watercolours of the dragon from the Book of Revelation that Blake painted for Thomas Butts, a government clerk who was his most loyal buyer for many years. The dragon waits for the woman to give birth so that it can devour the child.
VAULT-207: Masanobu was a publisher as well as an artist, and he claimed to have invented this kind of print. They were called 'floating pictures' because the European-style perspective, new to Japan, made the space seem to hang in the air. Here it is used for the inside of a packed kabuki theatre.
VAULT-200: One of six small witchcraft scenes Goya painted for the country house of the Duke and Duchess of Osuna, who were among his most cultivated patrons. The devil appears as a huge goat wearing a garland. Educated Spaniards of the time read such pictures as satire on superstition.
VAULT-209: Kiyonaga was the leading designer of prints of beautiful women in the 1780s, known for tall, calm figures. This scene of a public bathhouse had a notable later owner. Edgar Degas, who spent years painting women washing, kept an impression of it over his bed.
VAULT-210: Eisen specialised in prints of the courtesans of Edo's licensed quarter, shown in their heaviest and most expensive robes. One of his courtesans ended up on the cover of a Paris magazine in 1886. Van Gogh traced it and turned it into a painting.
VAULT-211: Muqi was a Chinese Zen monk of the thirteenth century. His work was valued far more in Japan than at home, and that is where almost all of it ended up. This small painting belongs to the Daitoku-ji temple in Kyoto and is very rarely shown. It is six persimmons, in ink, and nothing else.
VAULT-212: A hanging scroll nearly seven feet tall, painted around the year 1000, now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. A tiny mule train at the bottom gives the scale. Fan Kuan's signature was only found in 1958, hidden among the leaves in the lower right corner.
VAULT-213: Guo Xi was the favourite court painter of the emperor Shenzong. This scroll is signed and dated 1072. His son wrote down his father's ideas about landscape, including the advice that a painted mountain should be somewhere you could imagine walking and living.
VAULT-214: Huang Gongwang began this scroll in his late seventies and took about three years over it. In 1650 a collector who could not bear to leave it behind ordered it burned as he lay dying. A relative pulled it from the fire in two pieces. One half is now in Hangzhou and the other in Taipei.
VAULT-215: Night-Shining White was the favourite horse of the Tang emperor Xuanzong. Han Gan, who painted the imperial stables, shows him straining at a post. The seals and inscriptions crowding the scroll were added by its owners, emperors included, over more than a thousand years.
VAULT-216: A handscroll more than five metres long showing a day in Kaifeng, the capital of Song dynasty China, with hundreds of people, boats, shops and animals. In this section a large boat is about to hit the bridge and the crowd is shouting instructions. It is kept in the Palace Museum in Beijing and rarely shown.
VAULT-217: Shitao was born a prince of the Ming dynasty. When the dynasty fell his family was killed, and he was hidden and brought up as a Buddhist monk. In this self-portrait, painted when he was in his early thirties, he sits and watches a monk and a monkey plant pine trees.
VAULT-218: Mansur was the leading painter of animals and plants at the court of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who gave him the title 'Wonder of the Age'. He travelled with the emperor to Kashmir in 1620 and painted the spring flowers there. Very few of those flower studies survive.
VAULT-219: A page from the Blue Qur'an, written in gold on parchment dyed deep blue with indigo. It was made in the ninth or tenth century, probably in North Africa. The manuscript was later taken apart, and its pages are now spread across museums around the world.
VAULT-220: The oldest complete star atlas known from any culture, drawn in China around the year 700. It shows more than 1,300 stars. It was found in a cave at Dunhuang that had been sealed for about nine hundred years, and it is now in the British Library.
VAULT-221: The Book of Kells was made around the year 800 by monks of the community founded by Saint Columba. It was probably begun on the Scottish island of Iona and finished at Kells in Ireland, after Viking raids drove the monks out. It has been at Trinity College Dublin since the 1600s.
VAULT-222: The Lindisfarne Gospels were written and painted by one man, Eadfrith, a monk who became bishop of Lindisfarne, off the coast of northeast England. About 250 years later a priest named Aldred wrote an Old English translation between the lines. It is the oldest surviving version of the Gospels in English.
VAULT-224: Made around the year 1000 at the monastery of Reichenau, on an island in Lake Constance, which produced books for the German emperors. The emperor Henry II gave it to the cathedral he founded at Bamberg. It illustrates the Book of Revelation.
VAULT-225: A bestiary is a medieval book of animals, real and imaginary, each with a moral lesson attached. This one was made in England around 1200 and was in the royal library of Henry VIII by 1542. Tiny pinpricks around some pictures show how the artists transferred designs from one book to another.
VAULT-226: The Luttrell Psalter was made for Sir Geoffrey Luttrell, a landowner in Lincolnshire, who is shown here being armed by his wife and daughter-in-law. The book is famous for its margins, which are full of scenes of farm work and of strange hybrid monsters. It is in the British Library.
VAULT-227: The Voynich Manuscript is written in a script nobody has been able to read, with drawings of plants that match no known species. Its vellum has been carbon-dated to the early 1400s. It is named after Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it in 1912, and it is now at Yale.
VAULT-223: A carpet page is a full page of pure pattern, named for its likeness to an eastern rug. The Lindisfarne Gospels has five, one before each Gospel and one at the start. On the backs of the pages you can still see the compass holes and guide lines Eadfrith used to plan the design.
VAULT-229: Atalanta Fugiens, published in 1617, is an alchemy book by the German physician Michael Maier. Each of its fifty chapters has an engraving, a short poem, a commentary and a piece of music for three voices. It was meant to be looked at, read and sung at the same time.
VAULT-231: This picture is often taken for a medieval woodcut. It first appeared in 1888, in a popular book on weather by the French astronomer Camille Flammarion. Nobody knows who made it.
VAULT-233: Johann Bayer's Uranometria, published in Augsburg in 1603, was the first atlas to map the whole sky, including the southern stars that Europeans had only recently seen. Bayer also began the practice of naming stars with Greek letters, as in Alpha Centauri.
VAULT-234: The diagram that put the sun at the centre. Copernicus held the book back for decades and it was printed in Nuremberg in 1543, the year he died. The Lutheran minister who saw it through the press added an unsigned preface saying the idea was only a mathematical convenience.
VAULT-235: Galileo published this short book in March 1610, a few months after first pointing a telescope at the sky. It reported mountains on the Moon, many new stars, and four moons circling Jupiter. About 550 copies were printed, and they sold out quickly.
VAULT-236: The Codex Borgia is one of a small number of Mexican books that survive from before the Spanish conquest. It is painted on a long strip of deerskin folded like a screen, and was used by priests to read the calendar and foretell events. It is in the Vatican Library.
VAULT-237: One of only four Maya books known to survive. These pages track the movements of Venus and predict eclipses with great accuracy. The book has been in Dresden since 1739 and was damaged by water during the bombing of the city in 1945.
VAULT-238: The Codex Mendoza was painted by Aztec artists about twenty years after the conquest, for the Spanish viceroy to send to the emperor Charles V. The ship was captured by French pirates and the book ended up in Oxford. The eagle on the cactus, the sign that told the Aztecs where to build their city, is on the Mexican flag today.
VAULT-239: The Catalan Atlas was made in Majorca in 1375, in the workshop of the Jewish mapmaker Abraham Cresques. The crowned figure is Mansa Musa, king of Mali, holding a gold nugget. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, with a vast caravan and a great deal of gold, had made him famous across the Mediterranean.
VAULT-240: Piri Reis was an Ottoman admiral. This piece of his 1513 world map shows the Atlantic with the coasts of Europe, Africa and South America. In his notes he says one of his sources was a map used by Columbus. It was found in the Topkapı Palace library in Istanbul in 1929.
VAULT-241: Fra Mauro was a monk on the island of Murano in Venice. His world map, finished around 1450, is about two metres across and covered in thousands of notes drawn from travellers and merchants. South is at the top. It was the most detailed map of the world made in Europe up to that time.
VAULT-242: The largest medieval map of the world to survive, drawn around 1300 on a single calfskin. Jerusalem is at the centre and east is at the top. It hangs in Hereford Cathedral in England, which came close to selling it in the 1980s to pay for repairs.
VAULT-243: A medieval copy of a Roman road map. It is nearly seven metres long and only about a foot high, so the whole world from Britain to India is stretched into a ribbon. It shows roads, distances and stopping places, and was never meant to show true shapes. It is in the Austrian National Library.
VAULT-244: Gutenberg printed about 180 copies of his Bible in Mainz in the 1450s, and around 49 survive, some incomplete. The coloured initials and decoration were added by hand afterwards, so no two copies look the same. The Lenox copy, in the New York Public Library, was the first to reach America.
VAULT-245: Geoffroy Tory was a Paris printer and scholar. In Champ Fleury, published in 1529, he argued that the proportions of roman capital letters should be based on the human body. He also pushed for the accents, the apostrophe and the cedilla in written French.
VAULT-246: A two-page view of Nuremberg from the Nuremberg Chronicle, which was printed in that city in 1493. The printer, Anton Koberger, was the godfather of Albrecht Dürer. Many of the book's other city views are generic and reused for several places, but this one shows the real skyline.
VAULT-247: A page from one of Leonardo's notebooks, now in the British Library. He was left-handed and wrote from right to left in mirror image. The Codex Arundel is not a book he planned. It is a bundle of loose sheets from different decades, bound together after his death.
VAULT-248: The first plate of The Birds of America. Audubon insisted on drawing every bird life-size, so the book had to be printed on the largest sheets available, about a metre tall. He could not find a publisher in the United States and had it engraved and coloured in Britain. There are 435 plates.
VAULT-249: Basilius Besler was an apothecary in Nuremberg who looked after the garden of the Prince-Bishop of Eichstätt. His book of 1613 records it in 367 engraved plates showing over a thousand plants, arranged by the season in which they flower. It took sixteen years to produce.
VAULT-250: This is the earliest known photograph to show a person. Daguerre took it from his window in Paris in 1838. The exposure lasted several minutes, so the traffic and the passers-by on the busy street left no trace. One man stood still long enough to register, because he was having his boots polished.
VAULT-251: Nadar was a caricaturist who became the leading portrait photographer in Paris. He posed his sitters against plain backgrounds with no props. He also took the first photographs from a balloon, and in 1874 lent his studio for the first Impressionist exhibition. Gustave Doré was the most successful book illustrator of the century.
VAULT-252: Julia Margaret Cameron was given her first camera at forty-eight, as a present from her daughter. She turned a coal store into a darkroom and photographed her family, servants and famous friends, in a deliberately soft focus that other photographers criticised. This portrait of her was taken by her son Henry in 1870.
VAULT-253: One of the largest and finest Persian carpets in existence, about ten metres long. It is signed by Maqsud of Kashan and dated to 1539–40, and was made for the shrine of a Sufi saint at Ardabil in Iran. William Morris urged the Victoria and Albert Museum to buy it. Its twin is in Los Angeles.
VAULT-254: The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery in wool on linen, about seventy metres long, telling the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066. It was probably ordered by Bishop Odo, the half-brother of William the Conqueror, and stitched in England. Odo appears in it several times.
VAULT-255: Heinrich Schliemann found this gold mask in a grave at Mycenae in 1876 and believed he had found Agamemnon, the king who led the Greeks at Troy. The grave is in fact about three hundred years older than any likely date for the Trojan War. The name stuck anyway.
VAULT-256: Found in the 1920s in a royal grave at Ur, in what is now southern Iraq. One side shows war and the other a banquet. It is inlaid with shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli, which came from Afghanistan. Nobody knows what it was for. 'Standard' was the excavator's guess.
VAULT-260: Two young Frenchmen in London in 1533: the ambassador Jean de Dinteville and his friend Georges de Selve, a bishop. The smear across the floor is a skull, painted so that it only looks right when you stand at the side of the picture. The lute on the shelf has a broken string.
VAULT-259: Bruegel had travelled to Rome, and he based his tower on the ruins of the Colosseum. The king in the foreground is Nimrod, who according to tradition ordered the tower built. The city around it looks like Antwerp, where Bruegel worked. The painting is in Vienna.
VAULT-265: Kōrin made this as a close copy of Sōtatsu's screens, painted about eighty years earlier, probably by tracing them. The two never met. A century later another painter, Sakai Hōitsu, copied Kōrin's version in turn.
VAULT-266: A pair of screens covered in gold leaf, with the wind god on one side, the thunder god on the other, and the centre left empty. They belong to the Kennin-ji temple in Kyoto and are a national treasure of Japan. They are unsigned. Very little is known about Sōtatsu, who is thought to have run a fan shop.
VAULT-267: Pine trees in mist, in ink on paper, with most of the surface left blank. It is a national treasure in the Tokyo National Museum and regularly comes top when the Japanese public is asked to name a favourite painting. Tōhaku came from the provinces and competed for commissions with the powerful Kanō family.
VAULT-268: Kanō Eitoku was the favourite painter of the warlords who unified Japan in the late 1500s, and he decorated their castles with huge trees and animals on gold. Nearly all of that work burned with the castles. This was originally a set of sliding doors. He died in 1590, the year it was painted.
VAULT-269: From the oldest surviving illustrations to The Tale of Genji, painted about a hundred years after Murasaki Shikibu wrote the novel. The rooms are shown from above with the roofs taken off. Faces are reduced to a line for each eye and a hook for the nose.
VAULT-270: A set of four scrolls from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, kept by the Kōzan-ji temple in Kyoto. Rabbits, frogs and monkeys behave like people: wrestling, swimming, holding ceremonies. There is no text. They are often described as the starting point of Japanese manga.
VAULT-271: A handscroll nearly seven metres long, showing the attack on a retired emperor's palace in Kyoto during a rebellion in 1159. It is read from right to left, so the fire and the fighting build as you unroll it. It is in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.
VAULT-272: Haniwa are hollow clay figures that were set up in rows on the great burial mounds of early Japan. This warrior in full armour, from the sixth century, was found in Gunma and is a national treasure. It is in the Tokyo National Museum.
VAULT-274: From a three-volume book of erotic prints that Hokusai published in 1814. Nearly every major Japanese print artist made such books, which sold well and were widely owned. The writing that fills the background is dialogue between the woman and the two octopuses.
VAULT-276: Jeong Seon painted this in 1751, at seventy-five. It shows the granite face of Inwangsan in Seoul just after heavy rain, with mist still rising from the valley. It is a national treasure of Korea. In 2021 it was given to the National Museum of Korea from the collection of the late Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee.
VAULT-277: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an in 1974 found the first of them. There are around eight thousand life-size clay soldiers, buried to guard the tomb of the first emperor of China. They were originally painted in bright colours, and no two faces are the same. The emperor's own tomb has not been opened.
VAULT-278: The scroll illustrates a third-century text of advice on how women at court should behave. It is traditionally linked to the painter Gu Kaizhi and is probably a copy made a few centuries after his time, which still makes it one of the oldest Chinese silk paintings in existence. It is in the British Museum and is shown for only a few weeks a year.
VAULT-279: A bronze horse at full gallop, balanced on one hoof, which rests on a flying swallow. It was found in 1969 in a tomb at Wuwei in Gansu province and is about two thousand years old. It is now an emblem of Chinese tourism.
VAULT-280: The Mogao Caves are nearly five hundred Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff at Dunhuang, on the Silk Road. This cave holds a seated Buddha more than thirty-five metres tall, made in 695 under the empress Wu Zetian. The wooden front has been rebuilt several times, most recently in the early twentieth century.
VAULT-281: Giuseppe Castiglione was a Jesuit from Milan who arrived in Beijing in 1715 and spent fifty years as a painter to three Qing emperors, under the name Lang Shining. He combined European shading and perspective with Chinese materials and formats. This scroll is nearly eight metres long.
VAULT-283: Carved from a single piece of jade that was half white and half green, with the cracks and flaws worked into the veins of the leaves. Two insects sit on top. It is thought to have come into the Forbidden City as part of an imperial consort's dowry in 1889. It is the most visited object in the National Palace Museum in Taipei.
VAULT-284: A bronze cauldron cast nearly three thousand years ago. Inside is an inscription of about five hundred characters, the longest known on any ancient Chinese bronze, recording a king's instructions to his minister. It was dug up in Shaanxi in 1843 and is now in Taipei.
VAULT-285: A piece of banded jasper, carved and stained to look like a chunk of braised pork belly, with the skin, fat and meat in layers. It is shown next to the Jadeite Cabbage in the National Palace Museum in Taipei, and the two are the museum's most popular objects.
VAULT-286: The story goes that a tenth-century ruler, suspicious of his minister Han Xizai, sent a court painter to spy on his parties and paint what he saw. The scroll shows five scenes from one evening. The version that survives is a copy made about two hundred years later. It is in the Palace Museum in Beijing.
VAULT-287: Before paper, Chinese books were written with a brush on thin strips of bamboo, tied side by side with cord and rolled up. That is one reason Chinese was traditionally written in columns from top to bottom. The oldest known copy of The Art of War, found in a tomb in 1972, is on strips like these.
VAULT-288: Built in the early twelfth century for the Khmer king Suryavarman II and dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later became a Buddhist temple and has stayed one. It is the largest religious monument in the world, and it appears on the flag of Cambodia.
VAULT-289: Borobudur, in central Java, is the largest Buddhist monument in the world, built around the year 800. Pilgrims walk clockwise up through its galleries past more than two thousand carved panels on the life and teaching of the Buddha. It lay half buried under ash and jungle for centuries until it was cleared in the 1800s.
VAULT-290: A Hindu temple complex in central Java, built around 850. The three main towers are for Shiva, Brahma and Vishnu, and Shiva's is forty-seven metres tall. An earthquake brought most of it down in the sixteenth century, and it was pieced back together in the twentieth.
VAULT-291: Carved around 3100 BCE and found at Hierakonpolis in 1898. King Narmer wears the crown of southern Egypt on one side and the crown of the north on the other, so it has long been taken as a record of the country's unification. It is in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
VAULT-292: Found at Saqqara in 1850 and now in the Louvre. The statue is painted limestone, about forty-five centuries old. The eyes are rock crystal set in copper. The man's name is not known.
VAULT-293: Ptahhotep was vizier, the highest official in Egypt, under a king of the Fifth Dynasty, around 2400 BCE. A famous collection of advice on how to live is written in his name. This statue of him is in the Imhotep Museum at Saqqara, the burial ground where his tomb stands.
VAULT-294: The Prisse Papyrus is named after the French scholar who acquired it at Thebes in the 1840s. It holds the only complete copy of the Maxims of Ptahhotep, advice from an old official to his son, and is sometimes called the oldest book in the world. It is in the national library in Paris.
VAULT-295: Found in 1912 by a German team in the ruins of a sculptor's workshop at Amarna, the short-lived capital built by Nefertiti's husband Akhenaten. It was probably a model for other portraits, which may be why only one eye was ever inlaid. It is in Berlin, and Egypt has asked for its return many times.
VAULT-296: The mask is solid gold and weighs about ten kilograms. Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 and reached the mask three years later. The king had died at about nineteen. In 2014 the beard was knocked off by museum staff and glued back badly, and it had to be properly restored the following year.
VAULT-297: A map of the sky from the ceiling of a chapel in the temple of Hathor at Dendera, carved around 50 BCE. It mixes Egyptian star groups with the twelve signs of the zodiac, which had come from Babylon by way of the Greeks. A French team cut it out of the ceiling in 1821, and it is in the Louvre.
VAULT-298: A decree by Egyptian priests from 196 BCE, written out three times: in hieroglyphs, in everyday Egyptian script, and in Greek. French soldiers found it in 1799 and the British took it two years later. Because scholars could read the Greek, it gave Jean-François Champollion the key to hieroglyphs in 1822.
VAULT-299: Naram-Sin, king of Akkad, climbs a mountain over the bodies of his enemies, wearing the horned helmet that was reserved for gods. About a thousand years later an Elamite king carried the stone off to Susa as war loot and carved his own inscription on it. It was found there in 1898 and is in the Louvre.
VAULT-300: A stone pillar over two metres tall, carved with 282 laws issued by Hammurabi, king of Babylon. At the top he stands before the sun god Shamash, the god of justice. Like the Naram-Sin stele it was taken to Susa as loot in ancient times, and it was found there in 1901. It is in the Louvre.
VAULT-301: From the palace of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. The lions were kept in cages and released into an arena for the king to kill, as a show of his power to protect the land. The sculptors recorded the dying animals with great care. The reliefs are in the British Museum.
VAULT-302: The main ceremonial gate into Babylon, built around 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II. It is faced with glazed blue brick, with rows of bulls and dragons in relief. German archaeologists dug up the fragments in the early 1900s and rebuilt the gate inside the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.
VAULT-303: A clay cylinder buried in the foundations of Babylon after the Persian king Cyrus took the city in 539 BCE. In it he says that he let deported peoples go home and restored their temples. It is often called the first charter of human rights, though historians point out that such statements were standard for new kings. It is in the British Museum.
VAULT-304: The private palace of Darius the Great at Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Persian empire. Its dark stone was polished so highly that it became known as the hall of mirrors. Because the door and window frames were cut from solid stone, it is one of the best preserved buildings on the site.
VAULT-305: Completed in 691–92 by the caliph Abd al-Malik, and the oldest Islamic monument still standing. It was built over a rock that is sacred to both Jews and Muslims. The mosaics inside are original. The tiles on the outside were added by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman in the sixteenth century.
VAULT-306: The tomb of the conqueror Timur, also known as Tamerlane, in Samarkand. He built it for a favourite grandson who died in 1403, and was buried there himself two years later. Soviet archaeologists opened the grave in June 1941.
VAULT-307: A page from the Shahnama made for Shah Tahmasp of Iran, perhaps the most lavish Persian manuscript ever produced, with 258 paintings. It shows the first king, Gayumars, ruling from a mountain where people still dress in leopard skins. The book was broken up and sold page by page in the twentieth century. This page is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto.
VAULT-308: Illustrates a twelfth-century Persian poem by Attar. The birds of the world, led by the hoopoe, set out to find their king, the Simurgh. Thirty of them finish the journey and discover that the Simurgh is themselves. In Persian, 'si murgh' means thirty birds. The painting is in the Met.
VAULT-309: Built for Shah Abbas I from 1611 on the great square of his new capital, Isfahan. The entrance lines up with the square, and the mosque behind it is turned at an angle so that it faces Mecca. The tiles were painted in several colours on each square and fired once, which was much faster than cutting mosaic.
VAULT-310: Fath-Ali Shah ruled Iran from 1797 to 1834. He had many life-size portraits of himself painted, always with the long black beard and jewelled armbands, and sent them to foreign rulers as diplomatic gifts. This one is in the Hermitage in St Petersburg.
VAULT-311: Found at Mohenjo-daro, in what is now Pakistan, in the 1920s. It is only about seventeen centimetres tall. The name is a guess made by the excavators. The writing of the Indus civilization has never been read, and there is no clear evidence that it had either priests or kings.
VAULT-312: The top of a pillar set up by the emperor Ashoka around 250 BCE at Sarnath, where the Buddha is said to have given his first sermon. India adopted it as its national emblem in 1950. The wheel carved on its base is the one at the centre of the Indian flag.
VAULT-313: Found in 1917 on the bank of the Ganges near Patna. She is carved from a single block of sandstone and polished to a mirror finish. How old she is has been argued over, with estimates ranging across several centuries. The statue is in the Bihar Museum in Patna.
VAULT-314: About thirty Buddhist halls and monasteries cut into a curved cliff in western India over several centuries. They were abandoned and forgotten until 1819, when a British officer out hunting noticed an opening in the rock. The wall paintings inside are the oldest large group to survive in India.
VAULT-315: A carving of Shiva with three faces, about six metres high, inside a cave temple on an island in Mumbai harbour. It was cut from the living rock in the sixth century. The Portuguese named the island after a stone elephant they found there.
VAULT-316: One of the largest reliefs in the world, carved across two boulders at Mamallapuram on the coast of southern India. A natural crack between the rocks stands for the river Ganges coming down from heaven. The elephants are close to life size. Scholars read the scene in two different ways and have not agreed.
VAULT-317: A palace built on top of a rock two hundred metres high in the centre of Sri Lanka. King Kashyapa, who had taken the throne by killing his father, moved his capital here in the fifth century for safety. The way up passed between the paws of a giant lion built of brick. After his death it became a monastery.
VAULT-318: A thirteenth-century temple on the coast of Odisha in eastern India, built in the form of the chariot of the sun god Surya, with twenty-four carved stone wheels and seven horses. The wheels can be used as sundials. The main tower collapsed long ago, and what stands is the entrance hall.
VAULT-319: From the Akbarnama, the official history of the Mughal emperor Akbar's reign, illustrated in his own workshop while he was alive. This page shows his siege of the fortress of Chittor in 1567–68. As usual in the workshop, one senior artist drew the composition and another painted it. It is in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
VAULT-320: Akbar ruled most of northern India for nearly fifty years. He is thought to have been unable to read, and had books read aloud to him daily. He kept a workshop of more than a hundred painters, Hindu and Muslim, who between them created the Mughal style.
VAULT-321: A rare picture of the people who made the books. The emperor Jahangir ordered the painter Daulat to add portraits of himself and the calligrapher Abd al-Rahim to the last page of a manuscript made for Jahangir's father. They sit facing each other with their tools around them. It is in the British Library.
VAULT-322: Built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. It took around twenty thousand workers some two decades. Shah Jahan was later deposed by his son, and he is buried beside her.
VAULT-323: The tall stones at Aksum, in northern Ethiopia, marked the graves of its kings around the fourth century. Each is cut from a single piece of rock and carved to look like a building many storeys high, with a false door at the bottom. One was taken to Rome by Italian troops in 1937 and returned in 2005.
VAULT-324: The Church of Saint George at Lalibela, in the Ethiopian highlands, was not built. It was cut downwards into solid rock in the shape of a cross, about twelve metres deep, and then hollowed out. It is one of eleven such churches made there around 1200, and all of them are still in use.
VAULT-326: One of seven fired-clay heads found near Lydenburg in South Africa in the 1950s, first spotted by a schoolboy. They date from around 500 CE and are the oldest known sculptures from southern Africa. Two are large enough to have been worn over the head. They are in Cape Town.
VAULT-327: A small rhinoceros, about fifteen centimetres long, made of thin gold sheet that was once nailed over a wooden core. It was found in 1932 in a royal grave on Mapungubwe Hill in the north of South Africa, the centre of a trading kingdom in the 1200s. Under apartheid the find was given little public attention.
VAULT-329: The largest mud-brick building in the world. There has been a mosque on the site since the thirteenth century, and the present one was built in 1907. Rain wears the walls away, so once a year the whole town turns out to replaster it. The palm beams sticking out of the walls serve as scaffolding.
VAULT-330: Brass plaques like this once covered the wooden pillars of the royal palace in Benin City, in what is now Nigeria. About nine hundred survive. Nearly all were taken by British forces in 1897 and are now spread among museums, some of which have begun returning them. The guild that cast them still works in the city.
VAULT-332: A statue from Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, carved from hard basalt, where most of the island's statues are soft volcanic tuff. The back is covered with later carvings connected to the island's birdman ceremony. The crew of a British ship took it in 1868, and it is in the British Museum. The islanders have asked for it back.
VAULT-333: The largest ceremonial platform on Rapa Nui, with fifteen statues. They were pulled down during conflicts on the island, and in 1960 a tsunami scattered them inland. They were set upright again in the 1990s with the help of a crane donated by a Japanese company.
VAULT-334: Hawaiian feather cloaks were worn only by chiefs. Each is made of hundreds of thousands of feathers tied in bundles to a net of plant fibre. The red came from the ʻiʻiwi bird. The rarer yellow came from birds that had only a few such feathers each, which catchers plucked before letting the bird go.
VAULT-335: Malagan are carvings made on the island of New Ireland, in Papua New Guinea, for the ceremonies that complete the mourning of the dead. They can take months to make and are shown for a short time. Afterwards they were traditionally left to rot or burned, or later sold to outsiders.
VAULT-336: A cave in Patagonia, in southern Argentina, covered with hundreds of stencilled hands. The painters held a hand to the rock and blew pigment around it through a hollow bone. Most are left hands. The oldest are around nine thousand years old.
VAULT-337: Seventeen colossal heads made by the Olmec are known, from the Gulf coast of Mexico. Each wears a different helmet, and they are thought to be portraits of rulers. The basalt for the heads at San Lorenzo was moved from mountains more than sixty kilometres away, without wheels or draft animals.
VAULT-338: A carved granite shaft about four and a half metres tall, still standing where it was placed around three thousand years ago, at the crossing of narrow underground passages in the temple of Chavín de Huántar in Peru. It shows a figure with fangs and claws. The Spanish name means 'great lance'.
VAULT-339: The Nazca lines were made in the desert of southern Peru by clearing away the dark surface stones to expose the pale ground underneath. This figure is the monkey, with its spiral tail. The climate is so dry and still that the lines have lasted around two thousand years. What they were for is still debated.
VAULT-340: A stepped pyramid at Teotihuacan, the great ancient city near modern Mexico City, covered with carved heads of a feathered serpent. In the 1980s archaeologists found the remains of more than a hundred people buried beneath it, many with their hands tied, sacrificed when it was built.
VAULT-341: The Moche lived on the north coast of Peru and had no writing. Their potters made vessels in the form of individual human faces, so exact that archaeologists can recognise the same person portrayed at different ages. The stirrup-shaped spout is typical of the region.
VAULT-342: Cut from a single block of stone about three metres tall, at Tiwanaku in Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca and nearly four thousand metres above sea level. The figure over the doorway holds a staff in each hand. Early visitors found the gate lying on the ground and broken in two.
VAULT-343: A gold model of a raft carrying a chief and his attendants, cast in one piece. It shows the ceremony behind the legend of El Dorado, in which a new Muisca ruler, covered in gold dust, was rowed out onto a lake to throw offerings into the water. Farmers found it in a cave in Colombia in 1969. It is in the Gold Museum in Bogotá.
VAULT-344: A serpent with a head at each end, made of thousands of tiny pieces of turquoise fixed to a carved wooden base, with teeth of white shell. It was probably worn on the chest during ceremonies. It reached Europe soon after the Spanish conquest of Mexico and is in the British Museum.
VAULT-345: Electricity workers digging in the centre of Mexico City in 1978 struck this stone disc, which led to the excavation of the Aztecs' main temple. It shows the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui cut to pieces by her brother, the war god Huitzilopochtli. It lay at the foot of the temple stairs.
VAULT-346: A basalt disc about three and a half metres across and weighing some twenty-four tons. It was found under Mexico City's main square in 1790. It is often called the Aztec calendar, though it did not work as one. It shows the Aztec account of the five ages of the world, with the present age at the centre.
VAULT-347: Built around 1450 as a mountain estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, high above the Urubamba river in Peru. Its walls are made of stones cut to fit together without mortar. It was abandoned about a century later and the Spanish never found it. Local farmers led the American explorer Hiram Bingham to it in 1911.
VAULT-348: Aleijadinho, 'the little cripple', was the son of a Portuguese architect and an enslaved African woman, and the leading sculptor of colonial Brazil. A disease gradually destroyed his hands and feet. He is said to have carved these twelve prophets, late in life, with tools strapped to his arms.
VAULT-349: Tiradentes led a failed plot for Brazilian independence from Portugal and was hanged and cut into quarters in 1792. A century later, after Brazil became a republic, he was made a national hero. Pedro Américo painted this in 1893 and laid the body out to recall images of the dead Christ.
VAULT-350: Painted for the chapel of a monastery hospital at Isenheim in Alsace, where monks cared for people with a disease that caused burning pain and sores. Grünewald gave the crucified Christ the same marked skin as the patients. The altarpiece is in the museum at Colmar, in France.
VAULT-351: Bosch spent his whole life in the Dutch town of 's-Hertogenbosch, from which he took his name. Only about twenty-five paintings are accepted as his. This triptych, with paradise on the left and a much larger share given to hell, is in the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.
VAULT-353: From the same series of the seasons as The Harvesters. It was painted in 1565, after one of the coldest winters anyone could remember. The hunters are coming home with a single fox. The painting is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.
VAULT-357: Hans Baldung trained in Dürer's workshop and was close enough to him to be sent a lock of his hair when Dürer died. He settled in Strasbourg. Death surprising a young woman was a subject he painted again and again. This panel is in Basel.
VAULT-358: A portrait of the emperor Rudolf II as the Roman god of the seasons, built entirely from fruit, vegetables and flowers. Rudolf, who collected curiosities of every kind in Prague, is reported to have been delighted with it. Swedish soldiers took it as loot in 1648, and it is still in Sweden.
VAULT-359: Parmigianino was twenty-one. He had a carpenter make a curved wooden panel and painted himself exactly as he looked in a barber's convex mirror, with his hand huge in the foreground. He took it to Rome to show the Pope what he could do. It is in Vienna.
VAULT-352: Saint Anthony was a hermit in the Egyptian desert in the third century who, according to his biography, was attacked and tempted by demons. Bosch fills three panels with them. The painting has been in Portugal since the sixteenth century and is in the national museum in Lisbon.
VAULT-354: The archangel Michael and his angels drive the rebel angels out of heaven, and they turn into monsters as they fall. Some of the creatures are based on animals newly arrived from the Americas, such as the armadillo. The painting was credited to other artists until Bruegel's signature was found on it in 1898. It is in Brussels.
VAULT-360: Sánchez Cotán painted only a handful of still lifes, all set in the same kind of stone window, where food was hung on strings to keep it cool. In 1603 he closed his workshop in Toledo and entered a monastery as a lay brother. This painting is in the San Diego Museum of Art.
VAULT-361: A lamb with its feet tied, lying on a stone slab. Zurbarán painted the subject several times. To viewers in seventeenth-century Spain it was plainly a picture of Christ, the 'Lamb of God', though nothing in it says so. This version is in the Prado.
VAULT-362: Painted for the church of a charity hospital in Seville, where it still hangs. Death puts out a candle, and beneath it lie a crown, a pope's tiara, armour and books. The man who commissioned it, Miguel Mañara, was a nobleman who gave up his fortune to bury the poor and care for the sick.
VAULT-355: More than a hundred Dutch and Flemish proverbs, each one acted out literally in a single village. Several are still in use, such as banging your head against a brick wall and swimming against the tide. The painting is in Berlin.
VAULT-364: A real event. In 1749 Brook Watson, aged fourteen, was attacked by a shark while swimming in Havana harbour and lost his leg below the knee. He went on to become Lord Mayor of London and commissioned this painting himself. Copley had never been to Havana. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-365: In 1816 the French navy ship Medusa ran aground off West Africa. About 150 people were put on a makeshift raft and cut loose. Fifteen were alive when it was found thirteen days later. Géricault interviewed survivors, had a model of the raft built, and studied bodies in the hospital morgue. The canvas is about five metres by seven.
VAULT-367: A small figure on a strip of shore, with sea and sky filling the rest. Friedrich originally included ships and then painted them out. When it was shown in Berlin in 1810 the fifteen-year-old Prussian crown prince persuaded his father to buy it.
VAULT-356: Six blind men walk in a line, each holding on to the one in front, and the leader has already fallen into a ditch. Bruegel observed them closely enough that doctors have been able to identify several different eye conditions. It is painted in thin colour on linen and is in Naples.
VAULT-369: Pandemonium is the capital of Hell in Milton's Paradise Lost, a word Milton invented. John Martin's enormous scenes of disaster drew crowds in the early 1800s, though critics looked down on them. He also spent years drawing up serious plans for London's water supply and sewers.
VAULT-371: Ingres painted this in 1808 as a student in Rome, where he was required to send a study of the nude back to Paris. He enlarged it years later for exhibition. Oedipus is answering the riddle of the Sphinx, with the remains of those who failed at the bottom of the picture. It is in the Louvre.
VAULT-372: Moreau's version of the same story made his name at the Paris Salon of 1864. He has the Sphinx cling to Oedipus's chest and stare him in the face. It is in the Metropolitan Museum in New York.
VAULT-368: Friedrich painted this as a companion to The Monk by the Sea, and the two were shown and sold together. A line of monks carries a coffin into a ruined church. The ruin is based on Eldena Abbey, near the town on the Baltic coast where he was born.
VAULT-375: Millais painted the riverbank outdoors in Surrey over several months, then added the figure in his London studio. Elizabeth Siddal posed lying in a bath of water kept warm by lamps underneath. When the lamps went out she said nothing, and caught a severe cold. Her father made Millais pay the doctor's bill.
VAULT-370: Part of a set of three huge paintings on the Last Judgement, the last major work Martin completed. After his death in 1854 the three were sent on tour around Britain and to the United States, and large numbers of people paid to see them. They are in the Tate.
VAULT-376: From Tennyson's poem. The Lady lives under a curse and may only see the world in a mirror. She looks out of the window at Lancelot, the curse falls, and she gets into a boat to float down to Camelot, dying on the way. Henry Tate gave the painting to the gallery that bears his name.
VAULT-373: Shown at the Paris Salon of 1876. Salome dances before King Herod, for which she will be given the head of John the Baptist. The novelist Huysmans described this painting over several pages in his book Against Nature, which made it a touchstone for writers of the 1880s and 90s.
VAULT-379: Manet's last major painting, finished while he was seriously ill. The barmaid, Suzon, really worked at the Folies-Bergère, and posed behind a table in his studio. The reflection in the mirror behind her does not line up with what is in front of it, and people have argued about why ever since. It is in the Courtauld Gallery in London.
VAULT-380: The sitter is the artist's mother, Anna Whistler. Whistler insisted the picture was an arrangement of tones and that who she was should not matter to the public. In 1891 it became the first American painting bought by the French state. It is in the Musée d'Orsay.
VAULT-377: A later scene from the same poem Waterhouse had painted in 1888. This is the moment the Lady turns from her mirror to look directly at Lancelot. The threads of her weaving wind around her and the mirror cracks. It is in Leeds Art Gallery.
VAULT-374: A watercolour shown at the same Salon as Salome Dancing before Herod. The head of John the Baptist appears in the air before Salome. No one else in the room seems to see it.
VAULT-383: Félicien Rops was a Belgian artist who worked mainly as an illustrator and printmaker in Paris. This is his best-known image: a woman, blindfolded and nearly naked, led by a pig on a leash, walking over figures that stand for the arts. It is in the Rops museum in Namur.
VAULT-381: A firework display over a London pleasure garden. The critic John Ruskin wrote that Whistler was asking a large sum for throwing paint in the public's face. Whistler sued him for libel in 1878 and won, but was awarded a farthing in damages. The legal costs bankrupted him. The painting is in Detroit.
VAULT-384: In Greek myth the one-eyed giant Polyphemus falls in love with the sea nymph Galatea. Earlier artists made him a monster. Redon's looks over the hill at her as she sleeps. The painting is in the Kröller-Müller Museum in the Netherlands.
VAULT-386: Eve with the serpent around her shoulders. It caused a sensation when it was shown in Munich in 1893, and Stuck went on to paint about a dozen versions. He designed the heavy gold frames himself, in the form of an altar.
VAULT-387: Ensor imagined Christ riding into modern Brussels and nearly lost in a crowd of masks, banners and marching bands. Even the avant-garde group he had helped found refused to show it. It stayed in his house in Ostend for decades and was first exhibited in public in 1929. It is in the Getty Museum in Los Angeles.
VAULT-388: Munch painted several versions of this in the 1890s and also made it as a print. He showed it as part of a series on love, anxiety and death. One of the painted versions was stolen from the Munch Museum in Oslo in 2004, along with The Scream, and recovered two years later.
VAULT-390: The biblical heroine Judith, who saved her city by cutting off the head of an enemy general. Klimt shows her as a Viennese woman of his own time. The model is generally thought to be Adele Bloch-Bauer. The frame was made by his brother Georg. It is in the Belvedere in Vienna.
VAULT-394: Wally Neuzil was Schiele's model and partner for about four years. The painting was taken from a Jewish art dealer in Vienna in 1939. In 1998, while on loan to New York, it was seized by American authorities, and the legal case ran for twelve years before it was settled. It is in the Leopold Museum in Vienna.
VAULT-395: Franz Marc founded the Blue Rider group in Munich with Wassily Kandinsky in 1911, the year he painted this. He gave colours fixed meanings, and blue for him stood for the spiritual. He was killed at Verdun in 1916. The painting is in the Lenbachhaus in Munich.
VAULT-396: One of a series of Berlin street scenes Kirchner painted just before the First World War. The two women in the centre are prostitutes, and the men around them are possible clients. In 1937 the Nazi government removed more than six hundred of his works from German museums. This one is in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
VAULT-389: Munch called this Love and Pain. The title Vampire came from a friend, the writer Stanisław Przybyszewski, and it stuck. Munch said it was simply a woman kissing a man on the neck. He made several painted versions and many prints.
VAULT-391: Adele Bloch-Bauer was the wife of a Viennese sugar industrialist. The portrait, covered in gold and silver leaf, took Klimt three years. The Nazis seized it in 1938. In 2006, after a long court case, Austria returned it to her niece Maria Altmann, and it was sold to the Neue Galerie in New York for a reported 135 million dollars.
VAULT-397: The largest painting Kandinsky ever made, about two metres by three. He prepared it with more than thirty drawings and studies, then painted the canvas itself in four days in November 1913. It is in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.
VAULT-398: Malevich first showed this in Petrograd in 1915, hung high across a corner of the room, the place where a Russian household keeps its icon. The surface has since cracked badly. X-rays show two earlier compositions underneath. It is in the Tretyakov Gallery.
VAULT-399: A poster for the touring company of Le Chat Noir, a cabaret in Montmartre that had opened in 1881 and become the best known in Paris. Steinlen was Swiss, lived in Montmartre, and drew cats constantly. The name at the top is that of the cabaret's founder, Rodolphe Salis.
VAULT-400: The regulars of the Moulin Rouge. Toulouse-Lautrec put himself in the background, the short figure walking beside his very tall cousin. The woman with the green-lit face at the right was at some point cut off the canvas, and the strip was later sewn back on. It is in the Art Institute of Chicago.
VAULT-403: Beardsley was twenty-one when he illustrated the English edition of Oscar Wilde's play Salome. The drawings owe a good deal to Japanese prints. Wilde did not much like them. Beardsley died of tuberculosis five years later, at twenty-five.
VAULT-401: A poster for a small Paris music hall. The woman in black is the dancer Jane Avril, here as a member of the audience. On stage, with her head cut off by the top edge, is the singer Yvette Guilbert. Parisians would have known her at once by her long black gloves.
VAULT-393: Death stands on the left with a club, watching a cluster of people of all ages who sleep on, unaware. The painting won a first prize in Rome in 1911. Klimt later reworked it and changed the background, which had been gold, to dark grey-blue. It is in the Leopold Museum in Vienna.
VAULT-404: Salome holds up the head of John the Baptist. An earlier version of this drawing, printed in an art magazine in 1893, is what won Beardsley the commission to illustrate Wilde's play.
VAULT-407: Lavinia Fontana worked in Bologna and is often described as the first woman in western Europe to make a full professional career as a painter, with public commissions as well as portraits. She had eleven children, and her husband assisted in the workshop. This small self-portrait on copper is in the Uffizi.
VAULT-410: Judith Leyster was a member of the painters' guild in Haarlem by 1633 and ran her own workshop. After her death her name was forgotten and her pictures were sold as the work of Frans Hals. Her monogram was recognised on a painting in 1893. This self-portrait is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-411: Morisot's sister Edma watching over her baby daughter Blanche. It was shown at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, where it attracted little notice. Morisot could not sell it, and it stayed in the family until the Louvre bought it in 1930. It is in the Musée d'Orsay.
VAULT-412: The girl was the daughter of friends of Edgar Degas, and Degas himself worked on part of the background. Cassatt submitted the picture to the American section of the 1878 world's fair in Paris and was annoyed when it was turned down. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-413: An older man is led away by an old woman while a young woman on her knees reaches after him. Claudel had been the student, assistant and lover of Auguste Rodin, and the sculpture is usually read as his leaving her. She spent the last thirty years of her life in a psychiatric hospital and died there in 1943.
VAULT-409: Painted in London, where Artemisia had gone to join her father at the court of Charles I. In the art of the time, Painting was personified as a woman, with a gold chain and unruly hair. That gave Artemisia something no male painter could do: a self-portrait that is also the figure of Painting itself. It is in the British Royal Collection.
VAULT-417: Guan Daosheng is the most famous woman painter in Chinese history, known above all for ink paintings of bamboo. She was also a poet and calligrapher. Her husband, Zhao Mengfu, was the leading painter and calligrapher of the age, and the emperor collected work by both of them.
VAULT-414: Two dancers lean so far over that they seem about to fall. When Claudel first showed the group, with the figures nude, a state inspector refused to commission it in marble on grounds of decency. She added the swirling drapery in response. The composer Claude Debussy is said to have kept a cast on his piano.
VAULT-418: Wen Shu came from the most distinguished family of painters in Suzhou. Her great-great-grandfather was Wen Zhengming. She specialised in flowers, plants and insects, and for much of her life the sale of her paintings supported her household.
VAULT-419: Chen Shu painted landscapes, figures and flowers, and taught painting to her sons. One of them became a senior official and presented her work to the Qianlong emperor, who wrote poems on several of them. That is why so many of her paintings survive in the former imperial collection.
VAULT-421: Edmonia Lewis, who was of African American and Ojibwe descent, made her career as a sculptor in Rome. She showed this at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia. It then disappeared for about a century. At one stage it marked the grave of a racehorse at a track near Chicago. It is in the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
VAULT-422: Tanner studied in Philadelphia under Thomas Eakins and moved to Paris in 1891, where he spent most of his life. He was the first African American painter to win an international reputation. He painted this on a visit home in 1893. It is in the Hampton University Museum in Virginia.
VAULT-423: Dr Samuel Gross operating in front of his students at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. Eakins painted it for the 1876 Centennial Exhibition. The art jury rejected it as too bloody, and it was hung with the medical displays. In 2006 the city raised 68 million dollars to stop it being sold elsewhere.
VAULT-424: Homer's largest painting. In a hard Maine winter, starving crows have turned on a fox that is struggling through deep snow. It was the first of his works bought by a museum, the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, where it still hangs.
VAULT-426: Sargent painted this outdoors in an English village over two autumns. He wanted the light of dusk, which lasted only a few minutes each evening, so he would set up, paint fast, and stop. The girls are the daughters of a friend. The title comes from a popular song. It is in the Tate.
VAULT-427: The heavyweight title fight of September 1923 in New York. In the first round the Argentine Luis Firpo knocked the champion, Jack Dempsey, out of the ring and into the press seats. Dempsey climbed back in and won in the second. Bellows died a few months after painting it, at forty-two.
VAULT-428: A Victorian house seen from below, cut off at the bottom by a railway line. In 1930 it became the first painting to enter the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Alfred Hitchcock said it was a model for the house in Psycho.
VAULT-429: Saturnino Herrán painted Mexican people, customs and pre-Hispanic subjects in the years just before the muralists made them the centre of Mexican art. He died in 1918, at thirty-one.
VAULT-425: A man and three boys sail home with their catch in a stiff wind. Homer worked on it for three years and simplified it as he went, painting out a second boat and a fourth boy. It was shown at the Centennial Exhibition in 1876. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-430: Made by the Kwakwaka'wakw people of the Pacific coast of Canada. During a dance the wearer pulls hidden strings and the outer face, usually an animal, splits open to show a second face inside. From 1885 to 1951 the Canadian government banned the potlatch ceremonies at which such masks were danced, and many were confiscated.
VAULT-431: Dead and dying gladiators are dragged out of the Roman arena into the room where they were stripped of their armour. Juan Luna, a Filipino, won a gold medal with it in Madrid in 1884, when the Philippines was a Spanish colony. Filipinos in Spain celebrated the win as proof of what they could do. It is in the National Museum in Manila and is about seven metres wide.
VAULT-432: Hidalgo won a silver medal at the same Madrid exhibition of 1884 where his fellow Filipino Juan Luna won gold. At a dinner in their honour the young José Rizal gave a speech that is counted among the first public statements of Filipino national feeling.
VAULT-433: Raden Saleh was a Javanese nobleman who trained as a painter in Europe. Prince Diponegoro had led a five-year war against Dutch rule and was arrested in 1830 after being invited to negotiate. A Dutch artist had painted the scene as a surrender. Saleh's version shows the prince upright and angry. It was returned to Indonesia in 1978.
VAULT-434: Osman Hamdi Bey was a painter and archaeologist, and the founder of Istanbul's archaeology museum and its academy of fine arts. An old man in historical dress tries to train tortoises with a flute. It is often read as a comment on how slowly reform moved in the Ottoman Empire. It is in the Pera Museum in Istanbul.
VAULT-435: Laocoön was the Trojan priest who warned against bringing in the wooden horse, and was killed with his sons by sea serpents. The sculpture was dug up in a vineyard in Rome in January 1506. Michelangelo was among the first to see it. The Pope bought it within weeks, and it has been in the Vatican ever since.
VAULT-436: Found in 1863 on the Greek island of Samothrace, broken into more than a hundred pieces. The goddess of victory is landing on the prow of a ship. The head and arms were never found, though part of a hand turned up in 1950. She stands at the top of a main staircase in the Louvre.
VAULT-437: A bronze of a boxer sitting down after a fight, found in 1885 on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, where it had been carefully buried in ancient times. The cuts on his face and the drops of blood are inlaid in copper. His ears are swollen from old injuries. It is in the Palazzo Massimo in Rome.
VAULT-438: A Roman marble copy of a lost Greek bronze, made for the king of Pergamon around 220 BCE to mark his victory over the Gauls who had invaded what is now Turkey. The twisted metal ring around the man's neck and his moustache mark him as a Celt. It is in the Capitoline Museums in Rome.
VAULT-439: Built under the emperor Hadrian around 126 CE. The dome is forty-three metres across, exactly as wide as it is high, and is still the largest ever made of concrete without reinforcement. The opening at the top is the only source of light. The building became a church in 609, which is why it survived.
VAULT-440: Found in 1939 in a ship burial at Sutton Hoo in eastern England, crushed into hundreds of fragments. It has been reconstructed twice. The grave is thought to be that of Rædwald, a king of East Anglia who died around 624. The landowner, Edith Pretty, gave the whole find to the British Museum.
VAULT-441: King Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to hold the Crown of Thorns, which he had bought from the emperor in Constantinople for far more than the chapel cost to build. The upper level is almost all glass: fifteen windows, each about fifteen metres high, with more than a thousand scenes.
VAULT-442: A salt cellar in gold and enamel, made for King Francis I of France. The sea god guards the salt and the earth goddess the pepper. It is the only piece of goldsmith's work by Cellini known to survive. In 2003 it was stolen from the museum in Vienna, and police found it three years later buried in a box in a forest.
VAULT-443: A bronze sword found in a tomb in Hubei province in 1965. The inscription says it was made for Goujian, king of Yue, who ruled around 2,500 years ago. When it was drawn from its scabbard the blade was untarnished and still sharp. It is in the Hubei Provincial Museum.
VAULT-444: The Yungang caves, near Datong in northern China, were begun around 460 under the Northern Wei emperors, soon after a persecution of Buddhism had ended. This seated Buddha is nearly fourteen metres tall. The front wall of its cave collapsed long ago, which is why it now sits in the open.
VAULT-445: A gilt-bronze figure nearly a metre tall, made in Korea in the early 600s. The bodhisattva sits with one leg crossed over the other and a finger touching the cheek, in thought. It is a national treasure in the National Museum of Korea. A very similar figure in wood is kept in a temple in Kyoto.
VAULT-446: The central Buddha of the Longmen caves near Luoyang, about seventeen metres tall, finished in 675. An inscription records that the empress Wu Zetian gave a large sum from her own funds towards it. A long-standing tradition says the face is modelled on hers.
VAULT-447: The tallest stone Buddha in the world, seventy-one metres high, carved into a cliff where three rivers meet in Sichuan. A monk named Haitong began it in 713, hoping it would calm the dangerous waters. It took ninety years. Drainage channels hidden in the hair and robes have kept it from eroding.
VAULT-448: A Buddhist shrine on a mountain near Gyeongju in South Korea, built in the eighth century. It looks like a cave but is an artificial chamber built from hundreds of fitted granite blocks and then covered with earth. The Buddha inside faces east, towards the sea and the sunrise.
