VAULT-449: A bronze Buddha more than eleven metres tall, cast in sections from 1252. It was originally inside a wooden hall. The hall was destroyed by storms and, by tradition, a tsunami in the late 1400s, and the statue has sat in the open ever since. It is hollow, and visitors can go inside.
VAULT-450: A stone figure of the Buddhist goddess of wisdom, found in 1818 in the ruins of a temple at Singhasari in East Java. Local tradition identifies her with Ken Dedes, the first queen of the kingdom. The statue was taken to the Netherlands and returned to Indonesia in 1978. It is in the National Museum in Jakarta.
VAULT-451: The most sacred Buddhist site in Myanmar, on a hill in Yangon. The stupa is about ninety-nine metres tall and covered in plates of real gold. Tradition says it is 2,500 years old and holds eight hairs of the Buddha. In the fifteenth century Queen Shin Sawbu gave her own weight in gold to cover it.
VAULT-452: The keris is the traditional dagger of Java. The smith forges the blade from layers of ordinary iron and iron rich in nickel, sometimes from meteorites, and the pale layers show on the surface as a pattern called pamor. A keris is handed down in a family and is treated as having a character of its own.
VAULT-453: Han Fei was a prince of the state of Han who died in 233 BCE. His book argues that a state should be run by clear laws, strict punishments and reward, and should not rely on the virtue of its rulers. The king of Qin admired it, and went on to unify China. Han Fei himself died in a Qin prison.
VAULT-454: Carved a hundred metres up a cliff in western Iran. In it Darius the Great tells how he took the Persian throne, in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In the 1830s and 40s the British officer Henry Rawlinson climbed the cliff to copy it, and the copies made it possible to read cuneiform.
VAULT-455: The Great Stupa at Sanchi, in central India, was begun by the emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE. The four carved gateways were added about two hundred years later. The Buddha is never shown as a person on them. He is indicated by an empty seat, a tree, a wheel or a pair of footprints.
VAULT-456: Cut straight into a sandstone cliff at Petra, in Jordan, by the Nabataeans about two thousand years ago. It was almost certainly a royal tomb. The name comes from a local legend that treasure was hidden in the stone urn at the top, which is pitted with bullet marks from attempts to break it open.
VAULT-457: A small gold box set with garnets, found in the 1830s inside a Buddhist monument at Bimaran in eastern Afghanistan. The standing figures around its sides include one of the earliest known images of the Buddha in human form. It is in the British Museum.
VAULT-458: A gilded copper box found in 1908 near Peshawar, in the remains of a huge Buddhist monument built by the Kushan emperor Kanishka. It held three small pieces of bone, believed to be relics of the Buddha, which were sent to Burma. The casket is in the Peshawar Museum.
VAULT-459: A copper Buddha more than two metres tall and weighing about five hundred kilograms. A British railway engineer found it in 1861 while digging for building material at Sultanganj in eastern India. It is the largest metal figure of its kind to survive from ancient India, and it is in the Birmingham Museum in England.
VAULT-460: The largest of the temples at Khajuraho in central India, built around 1030. Its main spire rises thirty-one metres and is made up of eighty-four smaller ones. The walls carry several hundred carved figures. The erotic scenes the site is famous for are a small part of them.
VAULT-461: A large brass basin inlaid with silver and gold, made in Egypt or Syria in the early 1300s and signed six times by its maker. The name is a mistake. It was made decades after the death of Saint Louis of France. It was used for the baptism of French royal children, and it is in the Louvre.
VAULT-462: The main square of Samarkand, in Uzbekistan, framed by three Islamic colleges. The oldest was built around 1420 by Ulugh Beg, a ruler who was also an astronomer. The one opposite, added two hundred years later, has tigers and suns with human faces over its entrance, which is very unusual on a religious building in Islam.
VAULT-463: Built for the Ottoman sultan Ahmed I between 1609 and 1616, facing Hagia Sophia across a square in Istanbul. The name comes from the more than twenty thousand blue-patterned tiles inside. It has six minarets, which was thought presumptuous at the time, as only the mosque at Mecca had as many.
VAULT-464: A small mosque on the main square of Isfahan, built for Shah Abbas I and the women of his court. It has no minarets and no courtyard, because it was not for public use. When light comes through an opening at the top, a streak on the centre of the dome fans out like the tail of a peacock.
VAULT-465: A nearly life-size wooden tiger mauling a European soldier. A crank in its side works an organ inside the body, which makes the tiger growl and the man cry out while his arm moves. It was made for Tipu Sultan, ruler of Mysore. The British took it after he was killed in 1799, and it is in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
VAULT-467: Abanindranath Tagore, nephew of the poet Rabindranath, painted this in 1905 during protests against the British partition of Bengal. Mother India is shown as a young woman in saffron holding a book, sheaves of rice, a piece of cloth and prayer beads. The soft washes of colour owe something to Japanese painting.
VAULT-468: A granite slab about two metres tall from Chavín de Huántar in Peru. It is named after the Italian naturalist Antonio Raimondi, who in the 1870s found it in a farmer's house, in use as a table. The carving can be read either way up, and shows a different figure each way. It is in Lima.
VAULT-469: A pyramid forty-seven metres tall at Tikal, in Guatemala, built as the tomb of the Maya king Jasaw Chan K'awiil, who died in 734. Archaeologists found his burial chamber deep inside in 1962, with jade ornaments and a set of finely carved bones.
VAULT-470: Three rooms of wall paintings made in the 790s at a small Maya city in what is now Chiapas, Mexico. They show a court ceremony, a battle, and the torture and killing of prisoners. Outsiders first saw them in 1946. Until then many scholars had thought of the Maya as a peaceful people ruled by priests.
VAULT-471: In 1938 a man digging a water cistern at Igbo-Ukwu, in southeastern Nigeria, struck a hoard of bronzes. Excavations in 1959 found more. They date from the ninth century and are the oldest known bronze castings in West Africa. The casting is as fine as any in the world at that time.
VAULT-472: From the same site as the staff head. The lines on the face are scarification marks. Similar marks were still worn by titled Igbo men in the same region more than a thousand years later.
VAULT-473: A tumi is a ceremonial knife with a half-moon blade, made on the north coast of Peru. The figure on the handle is usually identified with Naymlap, the legendary founder of the Lambayeque kingdom, who was said to have arrived by sea. The tumi is now used as a national symbol of Peru.
VAULT-474: The main pyramid at Chichén Itzá, in the Yucatán. Its four stairways have 91 steps each, which with the top platform makes 365. Around the equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts a zigzag shadow down the north stairway that joins a carved serpent's head at the bottom. An older pyramid lies inside it.
VAULT-475: The largest earthwork in the Americas, about thirty metres high, at Cahokia in Illinois, across the Mississippi from St. Louis. It was built in stages from baskets of earth carried by hand. Around 1100 the city around it had more than ten thousand people. The name comes from French monks who lived nearby in the 1800s.
VAULT-476: An earthwork in the shape of a snake, more than four hundred metres long, on a ridge in southern Ohio. Archaeologists disagree about who built it and when, with estimates more than a thousand years apart. The head points towards the place where the sun sets at the summer solstice.
VAULT-477: The largest cliff dwelling in North America, at Mesa Verde in Colorado, with about 150 rooms. Ancestral Pueblo people built it between about 1190 and 1260. Within a few decades they had left, during a long drought. Their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and Arizona.
VAULT-478: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom that grew rich on the gold trade between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its granite walls, up to eleven metres high, were built without mortar. The white government of colonial Rhodesia long denied that Africans had built it. The modern country is named after it.
VAULT-479: Chan Chan, on the north coast of Peru, was the capital of the Chimú kingdom and the largest city built of mud brick in the Americas. Its walls are decorated with fish, seabirds and patterns like fishing nets. The Inca conquered it around 1470. Heavy rains now threaten what is left.
VAULT-480: An encyclopedia of Aztec life compiled over thirty years by the Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua students and elders. It has twelve books and about 2,400 pictures, with the text in Nahuatl and Spanish side by side. The last book tells the story of the conquest from the Aztec side. It is in a library in Florence.
VAULT-481: A wooden figure of a god from the island of Rurutu in the South Pacific, with small figures growing all over its body. It is hollow, with a lid in the back, and once held other small gods. The islanders gave it to British missionaries in 1821 as a sign of their conversion. It is in the British Museum.
VAULT-482: Ethiopian emperors traditionally ruled from a moving camp. In 1636 the emperor Fasilides broke with that and founded a fixed capital at Gondar. His castle and those of his successors stand inside one walled compound. The style mixes local building with ideas from Portugal and India.
VAULT-483: A long poem in Swahili about wars between the early Muslims and the Byzantine empire. The manuscript is dated 1728 and was written on Pate, an island off the coast of Kenya. It is one of the oldest surviving texts in Swahili, which at the time was written in Arabic script.
VAULT-485: Wooden figures of thin, bearded men with their ribs showing were carved on Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, and are thought to represent ancestor spirits. Men wore them hung around the neck at feasts. The wood is toromiro, a small tree that later died out on the island.
VAULT-486: Paul Revere in 1768, seven years before his famous ride. He was a silversmith, and Copley shows him in his shirtsleeves at his workbench with a teapot and engraving tools. Copley left Boston for London in 1774 and never came back. The painting is in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.
VAULT-487: Church put the viewer at the very edge of the falls, with no foreground to stand on. He showed the painting by itself in a New York gallery in 1857, and tens of thousands of people paid to see it in the first weeks. It then toured Britain. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-491: The model is Joanna Hiffernan, Whistler's companion. The painting was rejected by the Royal Academy in London and then by the Paris Salon. In 1863 it was shown at the Salon des Refusés, the exhibition of rejected works, where it drew as much attention as Manet's. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-492: Moema is a character from an eighteenth-century Brazilian epic poem, an indigenous woman who drowns swimming after the ship that carries her Portuguese lover away. Victor Meirelles painted her washed up on the beach. It is in the São Paulo Museum of Art.
VAULT-493: Bierstadt painted this view of California in a studio in Rome, and showed it in London and Berlin before bringing it home. It is not a real place. He combined features from different parts of the mountains. It is in the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
VAULT-494: Max Schmitt was a boyhood friend of Eakins and a champion rower on the Schuylkill River in Philadelphia. Eakins painted this to mark one of his wins. The rower in the middle distance is Eakins himself, with his name and the date on the side of his boat.
VAULT-488: Church travelled twice to Ecuador, following the route of the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt. The painting is three metres wide. In 1859 it was shown alone in a darkened room in New York, in a frame built like a window, and visitors studied it through opera glasses. It sold for the highest price yet paid to a living American artist.
VAULT-495: Whistler made the wooden bridge over the Thames much taller than it really was, a device he took from Japanese prints. The painting was produced as evidence when he sued the critic Ruskin for libel in 1878, and the judge asked which part of the picture was the bridge. It is in the Tate.
VAULT-496: The four daughters of an American couple living in Paris, painted in the hallway of their apartment. Sargent based the arrangement on Velázquez's Las Meninas, which he had copied in Madrid. The two tall Japanese vases belonged to the family, and now stand beside the painting in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.
VAULT-497: Two sailors take a reading of the sun at noon to work out the ship's position. Eight bells is the ship's signal for twelve o'clock. Homer painted it at Prouts Neck in Maine, where he had settled a few years earlier.
VAULT-498: On 7 September 1822, by the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo, Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent of Portugal. Pedro Américo painted the scene sixty-six years later in Florence, on commission. He admitted he had made it grander than it was. The prince was probably riding a mule. It is in the Museu Paulista in São Paulo.
VAULT-489: Church sailed to the waters off Newfoundland in 1859 to sketch icebergs from a small boat. He showed the painting in 1861, in the first weeks of the Civil War, and gave the entrance money to a fund for Union soldiers' families. It went to England and dropped out of sight until 1979, when it was found in a boys' home in Manchester.
VAULT-499: Students at the University of Pennsylvania's medical school commissioned this for the retirement of their professor, Dr Agnew. It is the largest painting Eakins made. Fourteen years after The Gross Clinic, the surgeons now wear white gowns and the instruments are sterilised.
VAULT-500: Remington was an illustrator of the American West who took up sculpture in 1895, and this was his first attempt. It was cast in bronze in large numbers and sold well. A cast has stood in the Oval Office of the White House under many presidents.
VAULT-501: A monument on Boston Common to the 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments to fight for the Union in the Civil War, and its young white colonel. Shaw and many of his men were killed attacking Fort Wagner in South Carolina in 1863. Saint-Gaudens worked on it for fourteen years.
VAULT-490: The volcano Cotopaxi in Ecuador in eruption, with smoke across the rising sun. Church had seen the mountain on his travels. He painted this in 1862, a year into the Civil War, and many viewers at the time connected the two. It is in the Detroit Institute of Arts.
VAULT-503: A summer evening on the Lower East Side of New York, with the street packed and washing hung between the tenement buildings. Bellows belonged to a group of painters who took the ordinary life of the city as their subject. The painting is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
VAULT-504: A portrait, without a face, of the poet William Carlos Williams, who was a friend of Demuth's. It is based on a poem Williams wrote after seeing a red fire engine with a gold number 5 rush past him on a wet night. His names and initials are worked into the picture. It is in the Metropolitan Museum.
VAULT-508: One of a group of sunflower still lifes Van Gogh painted in Arles in August 1888. He meant them as a decoration for the studio he hoped to share with his friend Paul Gauguin. This version is in the National Gallery in London.
VAULT-511: Michelangelo carved this between 1501 and 1504, starting when he was twenty-six. It stands just over five metres tall. It was first set up outside the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence and was moved indoors to the Accademia in 1873.
VAULT-512: Monet painted the harbour of Le Havre, his home town, at sunrise. He showed it in Paris in 1874 at the first exhibition of the group that became known as the Impressionists. A critic took the name from this painting's title.
VAULT-515: Manet painted this in 1863 and showed it at the Paris Salon of 1865, where it caused a scandal. The model was Victorine Meurent. The French state acquired it in 1890 after a public subscription organised by Claude Monet.
VAULT-516: Manet first called this picture Le Bain. The jury of the 1863 Paris Salon rejected it, and it was shown instead at the Salon des Refusés that year. The nude woman is thought to be modelled on Victorine Meurent.
VAULT-517: Rodin first made this figure for The Gates of Hell, a doorway based on Dante's Divine Comedy, where it sits over the doors. He made the first small plaster version around 1881, and it was enlarged in 1902 and cast in bronze many times. The cast in this photograph is at the Kunsthalle Bielefeld in Germany.
VAULT-518: Raphael painted this between 1509 and 1511 for Pope Julius II, in one of the rooms of the Apostolic Palace now called the Raphael Rooms. It gathers ancient philosophers, mathematicians and scientists in one hall. Plato and Aristotle stand at the centre.
VAULT-519: A double portrait, dated 1434, believed to show the Italian merchant Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini and his wife in their house in Bruges. The painter signed it on the back wall, above a round mirror that reflects the room. The National Gallery in London bought it in 1842.
VAULT-521: A Sunday afternoon at the Moulin de la Galette, a dance hall in Montmartre in Paris. Renoir painted it in 1876 and showed it in 1877. His friend Georges Rivière described the work on it in a memoir and named several of the people shown.
VAULT-522: Titian seems to have begun this between 1532 and 1534. Guidobaldo della Rovere bought it in 1538, the year he inherited the Duchy of Urbino. It was one of the inspirations for Manet's Olympia of 1863.
VAULT-523: One scene from the cycle of frescoes Giotto painted on the walls of the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua between 1304 and 1306. The chapel was built as a private chapel by the wealthy Scrovegni family and consecrated in 1305.
VAULT-524: The centrepiece of the Cornaro Chapel in the church of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, completed in 1652. It shows a vision described by the Spanish nun Teresa of Ávila, in which an angel pierced her heart with a golden spear. Bernini also designed the chapel around it.
VAULT-525: Klee made this in 1922, when he had been teaching at the Bauhaus for a year. It hung for several years in the Nationalgalerie in Berlin. It was declared degenerate art in 1933, and in 1939 the Nazi government sold it to a dealer; the Museum of Modern Art in New York bought it the same year.
VAULT-527: One of a series of nudes Modigliani painted in 1917 for his dealer Léopold Zborowski. It is believed to have been shown that year at the Galerie Berthe Weill, in the only exhibition of his work, which the police shut down. It sold at Christie's in New York in 2015 to the collector Liu Yiqian.
VAULT-528: Matisse painted this large panel in 1910 for the Moscow house of the Russian collector Sergei Shchukin, with a companion panel called Music. An earlier, paler version from 1909 is in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
VAULT-529: Three women gather the stalks of wheat left behind after the harvest, a right long allowed to the rural poor. Millet showed the painting at the Paris Salon of 1857. It is now in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.
VAULT-530: Constable painted this in his London studio in 1821 from sketches made on the River Stour in Suffolk, near Flatford Mill, which his father owned. The cottage on the left was the home of a tenant farmer, Willy Lott. Shown at the Paris Salon of 1824, the painting won a gold medal from Charles X.
VAULT-531: Donatello's bronze David was probably made for the Medici family in Florence. Its date is debated, with most estimates in the 1430s or 1440s. It is generally described as the first free-standing nude male statue made since antiquity. The photograph shows the head.
VAULT-532: This marble statue was found in 1820 on the Greek island of Milos, then part of the Ottoman Empire. It was presented to Louis XVIII of France, who gave it to the Louvre in 1821. It is usually identified as the goddess Aphrodite.
VAULT-533: The cave was found in September 1940 by four teenagers near Montignac in the Dordogne. Its walls carry about 600 painted animals, mainly horses, deer and aurochs, made around 17,000 years ago. The cave was closed to the public in 1963 to protect the paintings, and visitors now see replicas.
VAULT-535: Picasso painted this in Barcelona in late 1903 and early 1904, during what is called his Blue Period. The period followed the death of his friend Carles Casagemas in 1901. The Art Institute of Chicago acquired the painting in 1926.
VAULT-537: Miró worked on this painting for nine months in 1921 and 1922. It shows his family's farm at Mont-roig del Camp in Catalonia. Ernest Hemingway bought it in 1925, and his widow Mary gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1987.
VAULT-538: Duchamp painted this in 1912. He withdrew it from the Salon des Indépendants in Paris that year after the hanging committee objected to it. It was shown at the Armory Show in New York in 1913, where it drew wide attention and ridicule.
VAULT-540: Brâncuși made the first Bird in Space in marble in 1923 and went on to produce more than a dozen versions in marble and bronze. In 1926 United States customs officials taxed one as a manufactured metal object instead of admitting it free as art. Brâncuși went to court and won in 1928.
VAULT-541: O'Keeffe painted this in 1926, one of the large close-up flower paintings she began in the mid-1920s. It came to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1969 as part of the Alfred Stieglitz Collection. Stieglitz, a photographer and gallery owner, was her husband.
VAULT-542: Warhol painted thirty-two canvases, one for each variety of soup Campbell's then sold. They were first shown in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles. The dealer Irving Blum kept the set together, and it went to the Museum of Modern Art in 1996.
VAULT-543: Rivera began this composition in 1933 as a mural for Rockefeller Center in New York, titled Man at the Crossroads. It was removed and destroyed in 1934 after he refused to take out a portrait of Lenin. He repainted it that year at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City, the version shown here.
VAULT-545: Kahlo painted this double self-portrait in 1939, the year she and Diego Rivera divorced. It was shown at the International Surrealist Exhibition in Mexico City in January 1940. Mexico's National Institute of Fine Arts bought it in 1947.
VAULT-546: Magritte painted this in 1929, during the three years he lived near Paris. The line of French under the pipe says that it is not a pipe. The Los Angeles County Museum of Art acquired the painting in 1978.
VAULT-547: Pollock made this in the autumn of 1950 in his studio at Springs, on Long Island, with the canvas laid flat on the floor. He poured and flung the paint from above using sticks and hardened brushes. The Metropolitan Museum of Art bought the painting in 1957.
VAULT-548: Rothko painted this in New York in 1953. It belongs to the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles as part of the Panza Collection. Rothko was born in 1903 in Dvinsk, now Daugavpils in Latvia, and came to the United States as a child.
VAULT-549: Basquiat painted this in 1981, when he was twenty. He left it untitled, and it is often called Skull or Head. He had started out writing graffiti in New York under the tag SAMO, and he died in 1988 aged twenty-seven.
VAULT-550: Lichtenstein based this two-panel painting on a panel from the DC Comics title All-American Men of War, published in 1962. It was first shown at the Leo Castelli Gallery in New York in 1963. The Tate Gallery bought it in 1966.
VAULT-551: Escher first printed this lithograph in December 1953. Three sources of gravity act at right angles in the same room, so each group of figures walks on a different set of stairs. Escher was a Dutch printmaker who lived from 1898 to 1972.
VAULT-552: Banksy first stencilled this image on walls in London in 2002. The street versions have since been painted over or removed. In October 2018 a framed version shredded itself partway moments after selling at Sotheby's in London, and that work was renamed Love is in the Bin.
VAULT-861: A marble group carved in Rome between 1622 and 1625 for Cardinal Scipione Borghese. It shows the story from Ovid's Metamorphoses in which the nymph Daphne turns into a laurel tree as Apollo catches her. Bernini was in his mid-twenties when he made it. It has stayed in the Borghese collection in Rome.
VAULT-862: Painted in Rome in the later 1590s, when Caravaggio was living in the household of Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte. The picture went to the Medici in Florence. It lay unnoticed in the Uffizi's storerooms until the early twentieth century.
VAULT-863: Painted in Venice between 1520 and 1523 for Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, as one of a set of mythological pictures for a private room in his palace. It shows Bacchus leaping from his chariot towards Ariadne on the island of Naxos, where Theseus had left her. The National Gallery in London bought it in 1826.
VAULT-864: Repin painted this between 1870 and 1873, after travelling along the Volga and sketching the men who towed barges upstream. It shows eleven haulers harnessed to a boat. He was still in his twenties, and it was the picture that made his name. It is in the State Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg.
VAULT-865: Van Gogh painted his bedroom in the Yellow House at Arles in October 1888. He made two more versions in September 1889, while he was in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, one of them a smaller copy for his mother and sister. The three are in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.
VAULT-867: A woodcut made in Nuremberg in 1515. Dürer never saw the animal. He worked from a written description and a sketch of an Indian rhinoceros that had arrived in Lisbon that year as a gift to King Manuel I of Portugal. The king sent the animal on to Pope Leo X, and it drowned in a shipwreck off Italy before it arrived.
VAULT-869: Sargent painted this in Paris in 1882, drawing on a journey through Spain three years earlier. It shows a dancer performing in front of a row of guitarists and is nearly twelve feet wide. It was shown at the Paris Salon of 1882. Isabella Stewart Gardner acquired it in 1914 for her museum in Boston.
VAULT-870: Painted in 1913 by Franz Marc, a founder of the Blue Rider group in Munich. Marc was killed at Verdun in 1916. Soon afterwards the right-hand side of the canvas was damaged in a fire, and his friend Paul Klee restored it. It is in the Kunstmuseum Basel.
VAULT-871: Painted in London and shown at the Royal Academy in 1895, the year before Leighton died. He was President of the Royal Academy at the time. The picture dropped out of sight for much of the twentieth century. Luis A. Ferré bought it in 1963 for the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico, which he had founded.
VAULT-872: A large folding altarpiece of painted oak panels, completed in 1432 for a chapel in the church that is now Saint Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent. It was paid for by Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut. An inscription on the frame says Hubert van Eyck began it and his brother Jan finished it. One panel, the Just Judges, was stolen in 1934 and has not been found.
VAULT-873: A portrait of a young Florentine woman from a banking family, painted in Florence in the mid-1470s when Leonardo was in his early twenties. The juniper bush behind her plays on her name, since the Italian word for juniper is ginepro. The panel was cut down at the bottom at some point. The National Gallery of Art in Washington bought it in 1967 from the princely family of Liechtenstein.
VAULT-874: Ingres painted this in Rome in 1814 for Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples and sister of Napoleon. It was shown at the Paris Salon of 1819, where critics complained that the figure's back was too long. The Louvre acquired it in 1899.
VAULT-875: A series of about nineteen canvases showing the Palace of Westminster in London. Monet began them during stays in the city between 1899 and 1901, working from a terrace at St Thomas' Hospital across the Thames. All are the same size and show the same view in different light and weather. He finished them in his studio at Giverny, and many were shown in Paris in 1904.
VAULT-876: An image of a small patch of sky in the southern constellation Fornax, built up from exposures taken by the Hubble Space Telescope between September 2003 and January 2004. It was released in March 2004. It contains about ten thousand galaxies, some of them among the most distant then known.
VAULT-877: Painted in Paris in 1875 and 1876. The setting is the Café de la Nouvelle Athènes, and the two figures were posed by the actress Ellen Andrée and the artist Marcellin Desboutin. When it was shown in London in 1893 it was attacked in the press. It is in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.
VAULT-878: A portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, a young woman at the court of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, painted around 1489 to 1491 while Leonardo was working for him. The Czartoryski family of Poland acquired it around 1800. It is in the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków, and the Polish state bought the collection in 2016.
VAULT-879: This picture was long taken to be by Pieter Bruegel the Elder himself, from about 1560. Technical study has since led most scholars to think it is an early copy, by an unknown painter, of a lost original by Bruegel. The story comes from Ovid, and only the legs of Icarus are visible, in the water at lower right. The museum in Brussels bought it in 1912.
VAULT-880: A self-portrait painted in Paris in the mid-1840s, when Courbet was in his mid-twenties. He kept the picture all his life and took it with him when he went into exile in Switzerland in 1873.
VAULT-881: Degas modelled this figure in wax around 1878 to 1881 and dressed it in a real bodice, tutu and hair ribbon. The model was Marie van Goethem, a pupil at the Paris Opera ballet school. He showed it at the Impressionist exhibition of 1881, and it was the only sculpture he exhibited in his lifetime. The bronzes were cast after his death in 1917. The original wax is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-882: Painted in 1880 and 1881 on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on the Seine at Chatou, west of Paris. The sitters were Renoir's friends. They include Aline Charigot, whom he later married, holding a dog, and the painter Gustave Caillebotte, seated at lower right. Duncan Phillips bought it in 1923 for his collection in Washington.
VAULT-883: Dorothea Lange took this photograph in March 1936 at a camp of pea pickers at Nipomo, California. She was working for the Resettlement Administration, a federal agency that documented rural poverty during the Depression. The woman is Florence Owens Thompson, who was 32 and was not named publicly until 1978. The negative is in the Library of Congress.
VAULT-884: Carved around 1513 to 1515 for the tomb of Pope Julius II. The tomb was commissioned in 1505 as a much larger monument and was finished in reduced form in 1545, in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome. The horns on the head follow the Latin Bible of the time, which described Moses as horned when he came down from Sinai.
VAULT-885: David painted five versions of this portrait between 1801 and 1805. The first was commissioned by Charles IV of Spain. It shows Bonaparte leading his army over the Great St Bernard Pass in May 1800. He made the crossing on a mule, and he did not sit for the picture.
VAULT-886: Painted in Rome in the late 1590s. The subject is from Ovid's Metamorphoses: a young man who falls in love with his own reflection in a pool. The picture carries no signature, and it was first given to Caravaggio by the art historian Roberto Longhi in the early twentieth century. It hangs in the Palazzo Barberini in Rome.
VAULT-887: David painted this in Rome in 1784 as a commission for the French crown and showed it at the Paris Salon of 1785. The story comes from the Roman historian Livy. Three brothers of the Horatius family swear to fight three brothers from the rival city of Alba Longa to settle a war. It is in the Louvre.
VAULT-888: Taken on 14 February 1990 by the Voyager 1 space probe from about six billion kilometres away, as it left the solar system. The Earth takes up less than one pixel. The astronomer Carl Sagan had asked NASA to turn the camera back for the picture. It is one frame from a set of sixty that together show six of the planets.
VAULT-890: A photograph of columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, several thousand light years from Earth, taken by the Hubble Space Telescope on 1 April 1995. The astronomers Jeff Hester and Paul Scowen of Arizona State University made the image. New stars are forming inside the columns. Hubble photographed the same region again in 2014.
VAULT-891: Velázquez painted Pope Innocent X around 1650, during his second visit to Italy as painter to King Philip IV of Spain. The portrait has stayed with the pope's family and hangs in the Galleria Doria Pamphilj in Rome. From the 1950s the painter Francis Bacon made a long series of pictures based on it.
VAULT-892: Painted in tempera on panel in Florence around 1480. An inventory of 1499 records it in the town house of Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent. The figures are usually identified as Mercury, the Three Graces, Venus, Flora, Chloris and Zephyr. It has been in the Uffizi since 1919.
VAULT-893: A marble group commissioned from Canova in Rome in 1787 by the British collector John Campbell and finished in 1793. The story comes from The Golden Ass by the Roman writer Apuleius. Joachim Murat, Napoleon's brother-in-law, acquired it around 1800, and it is now in the Louvre. Canova made a second version, which is in the Hermitage.
VAULT-894: Turner showed this at the Royal Academy in London in 1844, when he was in his late sixties. The train is crossing Maidenhead Railway Bridge over the Thames, which Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed for the Great Western Railway. A hare runs along the track ahead of the engine. It came to the National Gallery with the rest of Turner's bequest.
VAULT-895: Painted around 1647 to 1651, this is the only female nude by Velázquez that survives. The name comes from Rokeby Park in Yorkshire, where it hung in the nineteenth century. The National Gallery in London acquired it in 1906. In 1914 the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed the canvas with a meat cleaver, and it was repaired.
VAULT-896: A series of more than thirty canvases showing the west front of Rouen Cathedral in Normandy. Monet began them in 1892 and 1893 from rooms he rented opposite the building, working on several canvases at once as the light changed. He finished them in his studio at Giverny in 1894. Twenty were shown together in Paris in 1895. They are now spread among many museums.
VAULT-897: Raphael painted this around 1512 to 1513 on a commission from Pope Julius II for the church of San Sisto in Piacenza. Augustus III of Saxony bought it in 1754 and brought it to Dresden. After the Second World War it was taken to Moscow, and it was returned to Dresden in 1955. The two cherubs at the bottom edge have been reproduced on their own since the nineteenth century.
VAULT-898: Painted in September 1888 at Arles, on the bank of the Rhône a few minutes' walk from the Yellow House where Van Gogh was living. The stars in the sky are those of the Great Bear. It was shown in Paris in 1889 at the exhibition of the Société des Artistes Indépendants. It is in the Musée d'Orsay.
VAULT-899: Painted in Rome in 1601 for the nobleman Ciriaco Mattei. It shows the moment in Luke's Gospel when two disciples recognise the risen Christ as he blesses the bread at an inn. It was given to the National Gallery in London in 1839. Caravaggio painted the subject again in 1606, and that version is in the Brera in Milan.
VAULT-900: A group portrait commissioned by the Amsterdam Guild of Surgeons and painted in 1632, soon after Rembrandt moved to the city at the age of 25. Dr Tulp was the guild's official lecturer in anatomy. The guild was allowed one public dissection a year, and the body had to be that of an executed criminal. This man was Aris Kindt, hanged for armed robbery. The Mauritshuis in The Hague has had it since 1828.
VAULT-901: Painted in Delft in the later 1660s. Vermeer never sold it, and after he died in 1675 his widow tried to keep it from his creditors. The model is dressed as Clio, the muse of history. Adolf Hitler bought it from the Czernin family of Vienna in 1940. It was recovered from a salt mine in Austria in 1945 and has been in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna since 1946.
VAULT-902: Photographed on 7 December 1972 by the crew of Apollo 17 on their way to the Moon, from about 29,000 kilometres out. It shows Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Antarctic ice cap, with the whole disc of the Earth lit by the Sun. NASA credits the picture to the three astronauts together. Apollo 17 was the last crewed flight to the Moon in the Apollo programme.
VAULT-903: The city of Calais commissioned this monument from Rodin in 1884, and it was unveiled there in 1895. It shows six leading citizens who offered their lives to Edward III of England in 1347 so that he would lift his siege of the town during the Hundred Years' War. Their lives were spared. Later bronze casts stand in London, Philadelphia, Paris and other cities.
VAULT-904: Painted between 1586 and 1588 for Santo Tomé in Toledo, El Greco's own parish church, on a commission from its priest. It shows a local legend. At the burial of Gonzalo Ruiz, a fourteenth-century benefactor of the church, Saint Stephen and Saint Augustine were said to have come down to lay the body in the tomb. The painting is still in the church.
VAULT-907: Delacroix showed this at the Paris Salon that opened in 1827. He took the subject from Lord Byron's play Sardanapalus, published in 1821, about an Assyrian king who has his possessions destroyed and dies on a pyre when his palace is about to fall. The canvas is about five metres wide. Delacroix kept it for many years, and the Louvre bought it in 1921.
VAULT-909: Painted in 1603 and 1604 as the altarpiece for a chapel in Santa Maria in Vallicella, the Chiesa Nuova, in Rome. French troops took it to Paris in 1797. It came back to Rome after the fall of Napoleon and went to the Vatican's picture gallery.
VAULT-911: In 1880 the French state commissioned Rodin to make a pair of bronze doors for a planned museum of decorative arts in Paris. The museum was never built. Rodin took the subject from Dante's Inferno and kept working on the doors until he died in 1917. The Thinker and The Kiss both began as figures for them. The bronze casts were all made after his death.
VAULT-912: A group of four watercolours that Blake painted in London between about 1803 and 1810. They belong to a long run of Bible illustrations he made for his patron Thomas Butts, a government clerk. The subjects come from chapters 12 and 13 of the Book of Revelation. The four sheets are now in American collections, among them the Brooklyn Museum and the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
VAULT-913: A three-panel altarpiece painted around 1512 to 1515. The centre shows a loaded hay wagon with a crowd fighting to grab from it, between a left wing of the Garden of Eden and a right wing of Hell. It is signed by Bosch. Philip II of Spain bought it in 1570. A second version is at the Escorial, near Madrid.
VAULT-914: A set of photographs taken in June 1878 at Leland Stanford's stock farm at Palo Alto, California. Muybridge set a row of cameras beside the track, and the horse set off each shutter in turn by breaking a thread. Stanford, a railway owner and former governor of California, paid for the work. The pictures showed that a galloping horse has all four hooves off the ground at one point in its stride.
VAULT-915: Painted in Amsterdam in the later 1660s, near the end of Rembrandt's life. The title dates from the early nineteenth century and has no basis in the record. Nobody knows who the couple are. Many scholars think they are shown as the biblical Isaac and Rebecca. The picture belongs to the City of Amsterdam and has hung in the Rijksmuseum since 1885.
VAULT-916: A set of six tapestries woven in wool and silk around 1500, probably in Flanders from designs drawn in Paris. The coats of arms are those of the Le Viste family of Lyon. Five of the six are generally read as the five senses, and the meaning of the sixth is still argued over. They were found in the château of Boussac in central France in 1841, and the Musée de Cluny in Paris bought them in 1882.
VAULT-917: Painted in Delft around 1657 to 1658. It is one of only two views of the town by Vermeer that survive. The oil magnate Henri Deterding gave it to the Rijksmuseum in 1921. In 2015 the historian Frans Grijzenhout used tax records to argue that it shows two houses on the Vlamingstraat in Delft, one of them lived in by Vermeer's aunt.
VAULT-919: Painted in 1850 by Ivan Aivazovsky, a marine painter of Armenian descent who was born and worked at Feodosia in Crimea. He was 33. The title comes from an old sailors' belief that waves grow in a series and the ninth is the largest. The canvas is more than three metres wide. It is in the State Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg.
VAULT-920: Painted on oak panel around 1567, two years before Bruegel died in Brussels. The bride sits in front of a green cloth hung on the barn wall. Which figure is the groom has never been agreed. The picture was in the Habsburg collections by the end of the sixteenth century and is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.
VAULT-921: Edward Steichen took this photograph in 1904 near the home of a friend at Mamaroneck, New York. He made the prints in platinum and added layers of coloured gum by hand, several years before a practical colour process was on sale. Only three prints are known. Two are in the Metropolitan Museum and the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The third sold at auction in 2006 for 2.9 million dollars, then the highest price paid for a photograph.
VAULT-922: Painted in April and May 1885 at Nuenen, the village in the southern Netherlands where Van Gogh's parents lived. The sitters were the De Groot family, farm labourers he had been drawing all winter. It was his first large composition with several figures. It is in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
VAULT-923: Matisse painted this in 1911 in his studio at Issy-les-Moulineaux, outside Paris. The pictures and sculptures shown in the room are his own works. It was included in the Armory Show in New York in 1913. The Museum of Modern Art bought it in 1949.
VAULT-924: One of Rembrandt's last paintings, made in Amsterdam in the years before his death in 1669. The subject is the parable in Luke's Gospel of the son who wastes his inheritance and comes home to his father. The canvas is more than two and a half metres tall. Catherine the Great bought it for the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg in 1766.
VAULT-925: Painted in Dresden in 1823 and 1824. Friedrich drew on published accounts of William Edward Parry's expeditions in search of the Northwest Passage, and on studies he had made of ice on the river Elbe. The stern of a wrecked ship can be seen among the slabs on the right. The picture was still unsold when he died in 1840. The Hamburger Kunsthalle bought it in 1905.
VAULT-926: On 2 May 1808 the people of Madrid rose against the French army occupying the city. Goya shows them attacking the Mamelukes, cavalry of Napoleon's Imperial Guard. He painted it in 1814, after the French had been driven from Spain, as a pair with The Third of May 1808. Both are in the Prado.
VAULT-927: Turner showed this at the Royal Academy in London in 1840 under the title Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhoon Coming On. It is generally linked to the Zong killings of 1781, when the crew of a British slave ship threw more than 130 enslaved Africans into the sea and the owners claimed insurance for them. The critic John Ruskin was its first owner. The Museum of Fine Arts in Boston bought it in 1899.
VAULT-928: Painted in Paris in 1897. Rousseau taught himself to paint and had worked for years as a toll clerk at the city gates. He offered this picture to his home town of Laval, which turned it down. It was given to the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1939.
VAULT-929: Courbet painted this in 1849 at Ornans, his home town in eastern France, after seeing two men breaking stones for road mending. He showed it at the Paris Salon of 1850 to 1851. It belonged to the picture gallery in Dresden and was destroyed in February 1945, when a vehicle moving it to safety was caught in the Allied bombing of the city.
VAULT-931: Painted in Paris around 1767 to 1768 for a private patron. According to the memoirs of the playwright Charles Collé, the commission was first offered to another painter, Gabriel-François Doyen, who refused it and suggested Fragonard. The fourth Marquess of Hertford bought it in 1865, and it is in the Wallace Collection in London.
VAULT-932: Ansel Adams took this photograph in 1942 in Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming. He was working for the United States Department of the Interior, which had hired him to photograph the national parks for a set of murals for its building in Washington. In 1977 it was one of the images placed on the Golden Record carried by the two Voyager spacecraft.
VAULT-933: Between 1905 and 1911 Klimt designed a mosaic frieze for the dining room of the Palais Stoclet in Brussels, a house built by the Viennese architect Josef Hoffmann for the banker Adolphe Stoclet. The mosaics were made by the Wiener Werkstätte in marble, glass, enamel and semi-precious stones. This is one of Klimt's full-size working drawings for it, which are kept at the MAK in Vienna.
VAULT-934: Painted in the autumn of 1889 at Pont-Aven in Brittany. Gauguin based the figure on a painted wooden crucifix in the chapel of Trémalo, just outside the village, and set it in the local landscape with Breton women in their caps. It is in the Buffalo AKG Art Museum in New York State.
VAULT-935: The first of Rousseau's jungle pictures, shown in Paris in 1891 at the Salon des Indépendants under the title Surprised! He never left France. He studied plants in the hothouses of the Jardin des Plantes in Paris and animals in the zoo and in books. The National Gallery in London bought it in 1972.
VAULT-936: Raphael's last painting. Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, later Pope Clement VII, commissioned it for the cathedral of Narbonne in France, and Raphael worked on it from 1516 until he died in 1520. The cardinal kept it in Rome and gave it to the church of San Pietro in Montorio. French troops took it to Paris in 1797. It was returned after the fall of Napoleon and is in the Vatican's picture gallery.
VAULT-937: A book of hours, a private prayer book, made for John, Duke of Berry. The three Limbourg brothers began it around 1412, and it was unfinished when they and the duke all died in 1416. Other painters added to it in the 1440s, and Jean Colombe completed it in the 1480s for the Duke of Savoy. Its calendar pages show the work of each month. The Duke of Aumale bought it in 1856 and it is at Chantilly.
VAULT-938: The oldest surviving photograph made in a camera. Nicéphore Niépce took it in 1826 or 1827 from an upstairs window of his house at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes in Burgundy. He coated a pewter plate with bitumen, which hardens in light, and exposed it for at least several hours. The plate was lost from view for decades until the historian Helmut Gernsheim tracked it down in 1952. It is at the University of Texas at Austin.
VAULT-939: Painted around 1660 to 1661. It shows Vermeer's home town from the south, across the harbour, with the Schiedam and Rotterdam gates along the water. It is one of two townscapes by him that survive. The Dutch state bought it at auction in 1822 for the Mauritshuis in The Hague.
VAULT-940: Painted in 1888 at Pont-Aven in Brittany. Breton women in their caps watch Jacob wrestling with the angel, the story from Genesis. Gauguin offered the picture to a local church, and the priest refused it. The National Gallery of Scotland in Edinburgh bought it in 1925.
VAULT-941: A pen and ink drawing on paper made around 1490, when Leonardo was working in Milan. It sets out the proportions of the human body as given by the Roman architect Vitruvius, with a man fitted into both a circle and a square. The notes above and below are in Leonardo's mirror writing. The Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice has owned it since 1822 and shows it only rarely because the paper is fragile.
VAULT-942: Painted in July 1890 at Auvers-sur-Oise, north of Paris, on one of the wide double-square canvases Van Gogh used in his last weeks. He died on 29 July. It is often called his last painting, but his letters show that he finished other pictures after it. It is in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
VAULT-943: Whistler, an American living in London, painted his mother Anna McNeill Whistler there in 1871. He called the picture Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1. It was shown at the Royal Academy in 1872. The French state bought it in 1891, and it is in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.
VAULT-944: A portrait of the painter's wife Amélie, made in Paris in 1905. It was shown that autumn at the Salon d'Automne, in the room that led a critic to call Matisse and his friends the Fauves, or wild beasts. The Stein family bought it from the exhibition. It is in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.
VAULT-945: Painted outdoors in 1875 at Argenteuil, on the Seine near Paris, where Monet was then living. The figures are his wife Camille and their son Jean, who was about seven. Monet showed it at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876. It is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
